paragraphs.text: 1 The word of the LORD that came unto Hosea, the son of Beeri, in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam the son of Joash, king of Israel.

Although Hosea is regarded chiefly as a prophet to Israel, that is, the northern kingdom, the Holy Bible dates his prophecy by the kings of Judah, mentioning only one of the kings of Israel. The man of God was called to serve the people of Israel and to warn them and forewarn them of captivity, yet his heart, enlarged with love for the salvation of all, rejoices in God's work with everyone, where God promises that "the children of Judah and the children of Israel [shall] be gathered together" [11]. He who serves God knows no limits to love, but desires to serve all and the salvation of everyone.

Some scholars see that Hosea mentioned only one king of Israel because the kings of Israel were wicked and unworthy of mention; he was content to mention this king who, though wicked, was honored with the title "saviour" (2 Kgs 14:27), and who was followed by a series of disturbances, assassinations and chaos that ended in captivity.

The prophet opens the book thus: "The word of the LORD that came unto Hosea the son of Beeri" [1], as though he wanted to affirm that what is in the book is not from himself but is "the word of the LORD," and he is only a bearer of the Lord's words and a true witness to them.

The prophet mentions his descent from his father "Beeri," which means "well." If Israel, as this book describes it, had become a ruined land, a barren wilderness, its fountain dried up and its spring withered (Hos 13:15), then it needs to sit with the Savior at the well, as happened with the Samaritan woman, to be refreshed from the spring of His water that never dries. What Hosea offers of words of salvation is from the divine well; whoever drinks of it shall never thirst (Jn 4:14).

2 When the LORD first spoke to Hosea, the LORD said to Hosea, "Go, take unto thee a wife of whoredoms and children of whoredoms: for the land hath committed great whoredom, departing from the LORD." 3 So he went and took Gomer the daughter of Diblaim; and she conceived, and bare him a son, Some may wonder how God commands His prophet to be joined to an adulterous woman as his wife and to beget from her children of whoredom, for He says to him: "Go, take unto thee a wife of whoredoms: for the land hath committed great whoredom, departing from the LORD" [2].

First: Some differ in interpreting the expression "a wife of whoredoms" (Hos 1:2); in English it is translated harlot and not adultress. Therefore some see that it does not mean merely an adulterous woman in the bodily way, according to the common understanding, but a woman who had consecrated her life to Baal, and so she is counted a harlot because of her attachment to Baal, especially since the worship of Baal was linked with the committing of adultery. There were women votaries who consecrated their lives to prostitution for the sake of Baal, and perhaps Gomer the daughter of Diblaim was of the class of these votaries.

In fact, the worship of idols was itself called adultery, harlotry, so that mere association with the worshippers of Baal was enough to give a person this title, even if he did not practice adultery. Perhaps this opinion is closer to the truth, for the majority of the Israelite women at that time, if not all of them, were attached to the worship of idols, so that it became difficult, perhaps impossible, for the prophet to find a wife except from among the worshippers of Baal, though not all of them practiced adultery bodily.

Second: A few scholars see that what is recorded in this chapter and the third chapter was only a vision or a symbolic story, presented to the people to reveal the ugliness of their fall and their turning away from the worship of the living God and their betrayal of Him instead of keeping the holy covenant with Him; and yet, with all this, God seeks them and wishes to bring them back to Himself, sanctifying them. But the majority of scholars see that what came here is a real event, and that God wanted the prophet to taste the great bitterness with Him because of Israel's deviation, and to declare to mankind the extent of God's care and love for man. As Abba Chaeremon says: [The divine Word described God's concern and care for us by the tongue of the prophet Hosea under the symbol of Jerusalem as a harlot, who turned aside in zeal full of ingratitude... He compares Jerusalem (the human soul) to an adulterous woman seeking another man, and compares His love for us to a man dying in love for his bride. For God's goodness and love are always declared to all men; they are overcome only by our ceasing to care for our salvation and by our fleeing from God's care for us, as though it were conquered by our evils. Therefore it is compared only to a man burning with the fire of love for his wife, who melts away in his love for her in proportion as he sees her treating him lightly and scornfully.]

Third: The majority of scholars see that the prophet married Gomer and loved her greatly, and then discovered what she was in the way of adultery (whether in the general bodily sense or merely association with the worship of Baal), and he kept her as his wife and did not divorce her; though some see that the prophet married her knowing her past, and that he consented to this because of the divine command, fulfilling in his life a symbolic picture of what was happening between God and His people.

Fourth: The word "Gomer" in Hebrew means the end of perfection, especially the perfection of failure, while "Diblaim" means a double cake of pressed figs or cakes of raisins. This kind of cake was used in the festivals of the worship of Baal, for it was said of the children of Israel that they "look to other gods, and love flagons of wine" (Hos 3:1), as though the eating of cakes stuffed with cakes of raisins or figs were closely linked with the worship of foreign gods. Thus the marriage of the prophet Hosea to Gomer the daughter of Diblaim points to his attachment to the people of Israel, who had reached the perfection of failure (Gomer), born of idolatrous worship and its abominations (Diblaim); or as though Israel, having become Gomer, is the daughter of Diblaim, that is, the daughter of the abominable festivals that spread throughout the land. She became like a cake offered to Baal, an abominable food and an unclean table for Satan and his followers!

Just as Gomer remained in her evil, bearing children of whoredom in spite of her marriage to a pure man and a blessed prophet, so Israel remained in its spiritual adultery in spite of God's declarations to it of His union with it. Hosea was not defiled because of Gomer; rather, Gomer came under a harsher judgment because of her marriage to the prophet unless she repented and returned in purity to her husband. So if Israel does not return to God in faith, its punishment will be more severe and more bitter!

St. Jerome sees in Gomer the harlot a symbolic picture of the Church, for he says: [What shall I say of the prophet's marriage to a harlot, who is a type of the Church gathered either from the Gentiles or from the Jews? She was first raised up by Abraham from among the worshippers of idols, and now she has denied the Savior and proved herself unfaithful to Him. Therefore she is deprived for a long time of her altar, her priests and her prophets, and remains many days until she returns to her first husband (Hos 2:7; 3:1), for when the fullness of the Gentiles comes in, Israel will be saved (Rom 11:25-26).]

And St. John Chrysostom says: [As in ancient times they took harlots as wives, so God received the nature that had played the harlot as His bride (without corruption), and the prophets declared from the beginning that this had happened with respect to the Jewish synagogue (Jer 3; Ezek 23:4-5, 11). But this bride was ungrateful toward her husband, whereas the Church, being saved from the evils she received from her fathers, continued to embrace her Bridegroom.]

The Lord says to Hosea: "for the land hath committed great whoredom, departing from the LORD" [1], and the Greek translation reads: "for the land hath committed great whoredom, departing from the LORD," as though whoredom were man's natural state when he leaves the Lord and is loosed from union with the eternal Bridegroom of his soul. It is remarkable that God does not say, "for Israel," but says, "for the land," and as we saw in the introduction, Israel, by bowing down toward earthly things, became an earth without heaven. I say that when we cleave to the dust we hear the divine voice: "for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return" (Gen 3:19), and we return to where the heart desired and turned. But if we put off the old earthy man whom we put on by our belonging to the earthy Adam, and put on the new man who is in the image of our heavenly Jesus, we hear the divine voice: "For you are heaven, and to heaven you shall return." I have borne the heavenly One in you, and your inner man has become heaven; therefore you return to where you desired and to what you have become, to heaven itself!

Since we have become earth by leaving the heavenly Bridegroom, what does this Bridegroom, who loves His bride, do with us? He took our earthy body, but without corruption, and came down to our earth to which our heart clung, without temporal things having any place in His heart, but to make of us "a new heaven and a new earth" (Rev 21:1), the earth of which it was said that righteousness itself dwells in it, that is, the heavenly Lord, the secret of our justification.

4 And the LORD said unto him, "Call his name Jezreel; for yet a little while, and I will avenge the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu, and will cause to cease the kingdom of the house of Israel. 5 And it shall come to pass at that day, that I will break the bow of Israel, in the valley of Jezreel." 6 And she conceived again, and bare a daughter. And God said unto him, "Call her name Lo-ruhamah: for I will no more have mercy upon the house of Israel; but I will utterly take them away. 7 But I will have mercy upon the house of Judah, and will save them by the LORD their God, and will not save them by bow, nor by sword, nor by battle, by horses, nor by horsemen." 8 Now when she had weaned Lo-ruhamah, she conceived, and bare a son. 9 Then said God, "Call his name Lo-ammi: for ye are not my people, and I will not be your God.

The Lord did not ask him only to marry an adulterous woman, but to beget from her children of whoredom, whose names God appoints: Jezreel, Lo-ruhamah and Lo-ammi. This does not mean that they were the fruit of adultery; rather, merely because they were born of an adulterous mother who was attached to Baal or to idolatry, they were counted children of whoredom, although they were the prophet's children, until they accept their father's message and reject the old spirit of their mother.

First: "Jezreel" means "God sows," the first child of Hosea and Gomer, and it indicates that the chastisements He sows in us are the fruit of our own work. Jezreel reminds us of what Jehu did to Joram the son of Ahab and the wicked Jezebel, who killed and inherited the field of Naboth the Jezreelite, and the dogs licked her blood in the very field she had seized (1 Kgs 9-10). She demanded the field by seizure and shed innocent blood to obtain it, so she received the desire of her heart; she received destruction in the same place, as the natural fruit of her actions. The Lord says of the children of Israel: "they were abominable like their love" (Hos 9:10). What man loves, he receives as its natural fruit. He who loved the passing earth and the corrupt desires of the flesh received corruption and became earth, and he who loved the heavenly, eternal God enjoys immortal life.

Second: "Lo-ruhamah" means (not pitied). When man does not have mercy on himself and falls under attachment to the worship of Baal, he cannot expect mercy from God, for despising God's longsuffering and mercy treasures up wrath against the day of wrath (Rom 2:5).

The Lord says: "For I will no more have mercy upon the house of Israel; but I will utterly take them away. But I will have mercy upon the house of Judah, and will save them by the LORD their God, and will not save them by bow, nor by sword, nor by battle, by horses, nor by horsemen" [6-7].

Israel was plunged into evil and withdrew from God its Savior; neither bow nor sword nor horses nor horsemen can save it. But Judah, which points to the Church of the New Testament, which is the body of Christ that came out of the tribe of Judah, has its salvation by the LORD its God.

He says of the Savior: "the LORD their God." On the one hand He ascribes Himself to them as their God if they are sanctified, taking pride in them, as He calls Himself the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob; and He does not ascribe Himself to the wicked, for He says to them: "I will not be your God" [9], and the Greek translation: "I am not Yahweh to you."

The Lord says: "I will save them by the LORD their God." The Speaker is the Father, speaking of the Son the Savior. As Father Novatian says: [If God says that He will save by God, and since He saves only by Christ, why should any man hesitate to call Christ God, since the Father declares it in the Holy Bible? Yes, if God the Father saves only by God, no one can be saved by God the Father unless he confesses that Christ is God, in whom and by whom God promises to grant His salvation.]

Third: "Lo-ammi" means (not my kinsman) or (not my people), for the word "ammi" in Chaldean means (people) or (tribe). If sin begets "no mercy," the bitterness of no mercy is the deprivation of man from belonging to God or God's not belonging to him. How can one who belongs to Baal belong to God? The most we enjoy is the delight of the new Jerusalem coming down from heaven (Rev 21:2), which is "the tabernacle of God with men, and he will dwell with them, and they shall be his people, and God himself shall be with them, and be their God" (Rev 21:3).

10 Yet the number of the children of Israel shall be as the sand of the sea, which cannot be measured nor numbered; and it shall come to pass, that in the place where it was said unto them, Ye are not my people, there it shall be said unto them, Ye are the sons of the living God. 11 Then shall the children of Judah and the children of Israel be gathered together, and appoint themselves one head, and they shall come up out of the land: for great shall be the day of Jezreel.

God mixes chastisement with hope, for He declares here that His chastisements are not absolute and that their rejection is not total but only for a time. He waits for them to return to Him so that He may restore them in more splendor and glory, restoring them as one strong and great kingdom, enjoying adoption to Him, rooted in Him, with Him as its head, for He says: "Yet the number of the children of Israel shall be as the sand of the sea, which cannot be measured nor numbered; and it shall come to pass, that in the place where it was said unto them, Ye are not my people, there it shall be said unto them, Ye are the sons of the living God. Then shall the children of Judah and the children of Israel be gathered together, and appoint themselves one head, and they shall come up out of the land: for great shall be the day of Jezreel" [10-11].

In the midst of the bitter chastisement He gives a new promise: He enters with them into a new covenant that was fulfilled not by their return from captivity but rather by their enjoyment of the Messianic age, and these are its features:

First: "The number of the children of Israel shall be as the sand of the sea, which cannot be measured nor numbered," as though He is fulfilling the promise He had earlier declared to Abraham: "and in multiplying I will multiply thy seed as the sand which is upon the sea shore" (Gen 22:17), the promise to which Jacob held fast: "And thou saidst, I will surely do thee good, and make thy seed as the sand of the sea, which cannot be numbered for multitude" (Gen 32:12).

Truly, "though he cause grief (by chastisements), yet will he have compassion according to the multitude of his mercies" (Lam 3:32); for in Christ Jesus our Lord the fainting soul and the dry bones are turned into an exceedingly great army (Ezek 37:10). She becomes, not like Jerusalem, "terrible as an army with banners" (Song 6:4), which the enemy of good with all his army and deceptions cannot ensnare for himself, but like many strong horses that draw the divine chariot in the procession of victory. Therefore her Bridegroom addresses her, saying: "I have compared thee, O my love, to a company of horses in Pharaoh's chariots" (Song 1:9).

The Apostle says: "one day is with the Lord as a thousand years" (2 Pet 3:8), and the believer also, who is like a passing day, becomes in Christ Jesus like a thousand years, bearing the heavenly mark (a thousand) with strong and mighty powers in the Spirit; so instead of a day he becomes countless years, and instead of human weakness he bears the possibilities of Christ: His mind, His will, His traits and His glory!

This is the mark of the Messianic age, which has turned our human life into "life in Christ Jesus"; instead of humiliation we have the inner heavenly glory, and instead of temporal thinking we live in the heavenly things.

Second: Mercy does not stop at abundance in number and strength in quality, but what rejoices our heart is our belonging to God as His sons: "in the place where it was said unto them, Ye are not my people, there it shall be said unto them, Ye are the sons of the living God." Instead of rejection we are counted sons and heirs of God, and joint heirs with Christ the only-begotten Son! We have become children of the living God, alive by our living Father. The Jews had called dead Baal their father and his wife Ashtaroth their mother, and so they bore the dead nature of their parents. This promise was not given to the Jews alone, whom He will receive after their rejection at the end of the ages when they accept the Messiah the Savior, but it touches our life, we who are of Gentile origin, for we were rejected because of our rejection of Him, and now the door of sonship to Him has been opened to us. As St. Augustine says: [Even the Apostle understood this saying as a prophetic testimony concerning the calling of the Gentiles, who before did not belong to God. And since this people from the Gentiles became children of Abraham spiritually, they were rightly called "Israel," and therefore he goes on to say: "Then shall the children of Judah and the children of Israel be gathered together, and appoint themselves one head."]

Third: God's surpassing mercies in the Messianic age are declared through our unity together in Christ Jesus the one Head, "and appoint themselves one head." By accepting faith in Christ Jesus and enjoying adoption to God through Baptism, they appoint themselves one head.

He does not say, "They gather together under one king," but He highlights the perfection of unity by the Savior's being a Head from whom the body cannot be separated! It is a surpassing love, and a bond between the Creator and His beloved creation that cannot be expressed!

Fourth: We are joined together in the heavenly Head, so we bear His upper nature and ascend from our earthy, earthly nature, for He says: "and they shall come up out of the land." As the Apostle says: "If ye then be risen with Christ, seek those things which are above, where Christ sitteth on the right hand of God. Set your affection on things above, not on things on the earth" (Col 3:1-2), since we are not of the world (Jn 15:19), but our conversation is in heaven (Phil 3:20).

In Christ Jesus we ascend from our old earthly nature, to enjoy the new heavenly nature that is in the image of our Creator, truly singing: "Come ye, and let us go up to the mountain of the LORD." It is an exodus not from the land of Egypt toward the promised land, but a new ascent from the earth that enslaved the soul and in which it accepted Pharaoh (the devil) as a king who humbles the people. It is an ascent under the leadership of the Lord Christ Himself, not to take us to Mount Sinai, where there are lightnings and thunders and the smoking mountain, but for union with the Lord Christ, the holy mountain, that He may bring us by His Holy Spirit into the bosom of His Father.

Fifth: He concludes the promise by saying: "for great shall be the day of Jezreel." After "Jezreel" represented a threat and bitterness, where God gives us the fruit of our sins as chastisement for us, "Jezreel" becomes a promise, for the word means "God sows," so He sows us with His own hands as a new, holy planting (Isa 6:13); He sows us as members of the body of His only-begotten Son, we are watered with the waters of the Holy Spirit and bear the righteousness of Christ within us. He feeds us from the pierced side, so that we draw the very life instead of the death that was ours. This is what God assures us: "And I will sow her unto me in the earth; and I will have mercy upon Lo-ruhamah; and I will say to Lo-ammi, Thou art my people; and he shall say, Thou art my God" (Hos 2:23).

1 "Say ye unto your brethren, Ammi; and to your sisters, Ruhamah. 2 Plead with your mother, plead: for she is not my wife, neither am I her husband: let her therefore put away her whoredoms out of her sight, and her adulteries from between her breasts; 3 Lest I strip her naked, and set her as in the day that she was born, and make her as a wilderness, and set her like a dry land, and slay her with thirst. 4 And I will not have mercy upon her children; for they be the children of whoredoms.

"Say ye unto your brethren, Ammi; and to your sisters, Ruhamah. Plead with your mother, plead: for she is not my wife, neither am I her husband: let her therefore put away her whoredoms out of her sight, and her adulteries from between her breasts" [1-2].

Since God declared of this nation that it had committed adultery by leaving its true God to unite its heart with Baal, He could not call it His wife, for it had betrayed Him and He had divorced it; rather He calls it "their mother," in order to rouse it to repentance and to return to Him, on the collective level as well as on the personal level of each member in it.

And with all the evil it had done, the Lord opens His speech by the prophet, as He closes it, with the declaration of renewing the covenant with them, announcing that they are His people and the object of His mercy. In this spirit the Apostle Paul says: "Brethren, my heart's desire and prayer to God for Israel is, that they might be saved" (Rom 10:1).

To whom is the speech directed: "Say ye unto your brethren, Ammi; and to your sisters, Ruhamah"? Although Gomer the daughter of Diblaim bears Jezreel, Lo-ruhamah and Lo-ammi, there is a small remnant in the midst of the people who are holy to God, or at least longing for a life holy to the Lord. To these God directs His speech, that they may open the doors of hope before their fallen brethren and declare that God longs to gather them so that they may become His people and that He may have mercy on them, but not without sanctification or striving, for He says: "Plead."

Let them plead with their mother, who lost her belonging to God and is no longer His wife because of her adultery and whoredom. It is a trial that takes place within the circle of the soul by the Holy Spirit, so that man judges himself before he is exposed on the great day of the Lord. Let each one say to himself: "Plead with your mother, plead," so that we judge ourselves before we are judged. May we not be silent about the corruption of the bride who belongs to the Lord, but let us repeat to ourselves what St. Basil the Great wrote to a fallen virgin: [If John rebuked boldly, even to death, when he saw a marriage that ought not to have been, how much more would his feelings be when he sees the violation of a marriage belonging to the Lord! You have cast off from you the yoke of divine union. You have fled from the holy bridal chamber of the true King. You have fallen into that corrupt, defiled ruin... Who would not grieve over such things, saying: "How is the faithful city become an harlot" (Isa 1:21)?!]

As for the purpose of this trial, it is: "let her therefore put away her whoredoms out of her sight, and her adulteries from between her breasts" [2]. For when we judge ourselves we remove shamelessness from our face, so that we are ashamed of our weakness and seek to be covered by His grace; then we hear our heavenly Bridegroom saying: "Arise, my love, my fair one, and come away. O my dove, that art in the clefts of the rock, in the secret places of the stairs, let me see thy countenance, let me hear thy voice; for sweet is thy voice, and thy countenance is comely" (Song 2:13-14). He grants us the power of His resurrection, saying: "Arise," so we die to every uncleanness that stained our face, and His divine traits appear in His eyes, glorified by His resurrection and adorned by the work of His Holy Spirit.

May He remove by His Holy Spirit the adulteries from between the breasts, that is, from within the heart, so that we may say to Him: "He shall lie all night betwixt my breasts" (Song 1:13), for the Holy One cannot lodge where adultery settles, for what fellowship hath light with darkness? and what concord hath the Lord Christ with Belial?

What does removing adultery from the breasts mean? If the heavenly Bridegroom has two breasts, which are the Old and New Testaments, they are also the breasts of the bride, as they are the book of the Church, so it is fitting for the bride to present them through her holy life in the Lord, and for no one to corrupt their message by his evil life, causing others to stumble from enjoying them as food for souls. In this sense St. Jerome wrote to the monk Pammachius, encouraging him to study the Holy Bible, saying: [Give him your breasts to suck from your pierced bosom, and let him rest in his inheritance (Ps 68:13).]

If we judge ourselves we are not judged, but if we are lax with ourselves in the matter of sin, we fall under this sentence: "Lest I strip her naked, and set her as in the day that she was born, and make her as a wilderness, and set her like a dry land, and slay her with thirst. And I will not have mercy upon her children; for they be the children of whoredoms" [3-4].

What does He mean by saying, "Lest I strip her naked, and set her as in the day that she was born," except that since she left Him by her own will, He does not compel her to be joined to Him, so she loses Him as the covering of her inner life? She rejects Him, so she loses Him as a robe of righteousness with which she is clothed, and she appears in her corrupt nature as on the day of her bodily birth, with nothing to cover her weakness. She has deprived herself, by herself, of the Lord Christ, whom we put on, as the Apostle Paul says: (Gal 3:27).

As for His saying, "make her as a wilderness, and set her like a dry land, and slay her with thirst," it is because she rejects God, so she does not receive His Holy Spirit, who comes down upon our barren earth like rain to water it and makes its arid wilderness a fruitful paradise, so that she may say to her Bridegroom: "Let my beloved come into his garden, and eat his pleasant fruits" (Song 4:16).

As for His saying, "And I will not have mercy upon her children; for they be the children of whoredoms," it points to the fruit that springs in us from ourselves and not from our union with the heavenly Bridegroom; of this the Lord Christ said that every plant which His heavenly Father has not planted shall be rooted up (Mt 15:13), for it is a stranger to the Kingdom of God and deserves only to be burned! These works that are not of God are "children of whoredoms," while the works that are of God's planting are bound to Him, untouched by the evil one, but remain accompanying us throughout our eternity, as the Church says: "Write, Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord from henceforth: Yea, saith the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours; and their works do follow them" (Rev 14:13).

5 "For their mother hath played the harlot: she that conceived them hath done shamefully: for she said, I will go after my lovers, that give me my bread and my water, my wool and my flax, mine oil and my drink. 6 Therefore, behold, I will hedge up thy way with thorns, and make a wall, that she shall not find her paths. 7 And she shall follow after her lovers, but she shall not overtake them; and she shall seek them, but shall not find them: then shall she say, I will go and return to my first husband; for then was it better with me than now.

As God seeks His bride, threatening her if she refuses, or rather warning her lest she become naked and a wilderness and not enjoy His mercy, He reveals to her that what happens to her is not out of cruelty on His part but is the natural fruit of her leaving the truth, the secret of her life and her satisfaction, and her running after vanity, which offers nothing but death and deprivation.

He says: "For their mother hath played the harlot: she that conceived them hath done shamefully: for she said, I will go after my lovers, that give me my bread and my water, my wool and my flax, mine oil and my drink" [5]. He has made clear that the secret of her ruin is her adultery and her committing of shame, not in the general bodily sense, but committing it first inwardly in the heart, where she places her needs with them: they provide her food (my bread), her drink (my water), her clothing (my wool and my flax), her medicines (my oil), and her delight (my drink). This is spiritual adultery, where man leans on another than God, the Bridegroom of his soul, to ask from him his needs and find in him his satisfaction and pleasure. And as God works to bring us back to Himself, He tightens the pressure around us so that we realize that our running after others offers us nothing but a mirage, for He says: "Therefore, behold, I will hedge up thy way with thorns, and make a wall, that she shall not find her paths. And she shall follow after her lovers, but she shall not overtake them; and she shall seek them, but shall not find them" [7]. If sin brings man "thorns also and thistles" (Gen 3:18), and as the wise man says: "Thorns and snares are in the way of the froward" (Prov 22:5), then God in His love lets these thorns block our way, that perhaps we may realize our error and return to Him. When it is said that God is froward with the froward (Ps 18:36), and "walk[s] contrary" to those who walk contrary to Him (Lev 26:23-24), He does so as the natural fruit of our evil, so that we reap the fruit of evil, and at the same time as a sign of divine love for our chastisement, that we may turn back from our way. If we do not care, He sets up for us a wall of afflictions and toils to close our crooked way before us, and we realize that our striving in it is vain.

Through this affliction we realize the vanity of our running after others, for we draw near to the lovers but do not overtake them, and we seek them but do not find them. Who are these lovers? Perhaps He meant by them the king of Assyria and the Pharaoh of Egypt and those like them, for an alliance with one of them for fear of another is a vain alliance, for these work for their own interest and exploit Israel and Judah without helping them in the time of distress. They are like "the staff of this bruised reed" (2 Kgs 18:21). Perhaps by the lovers He also meant Baal and Ashtaroth and the sorcery that accompanied idolatrous worship... all of which Israel dedicated its life, its energies and all its feelings to, although they cannot rescue or save it.

The purpose of these troubles is the return of the bride to her wise attachment, so that she leaves her adultery and returns to her true husband: "then shall she say, I will go and return to my first husband; for then was it better with me than now" [7], as though she were the prodigal son who said: "I will arise and go to my father" (Lk 15:18).

8 "For she did not know that I gave her corn, and wine, and oil, and multiplied her silver and gold, which they prepared for Baal. 9 Therefore will I return, and take away my corn in the time thereof, and my wine in the season thereof, and will recover my wool and my flax given to cover her nakedness. 10 And now will I discover her lewdness in the sight of her lovers, and none shall deliver her out of mine hand. 11 I will also cause all her mirth to cease, her feast days, her new moons, and her sabbaths, and all her solemn feasts. 12 And I will destroy her vines and her fig trees, whereof she hath said, These are my rewards that my lovers have given me: and I will make them a forest, and the beasts of the field shall eat them. 13 And I will visit upon her the days of Baalim, wherein she burned incense to them, and she decked herself with her earrings and her jewels, and she went after her lovers, and forgat me, saith the LORD.

In our study of the book of Ezekiel we saw God rebuking His bride not only because she was unfaithful but because she took His riches and His holy things to use them in her betrayal of Him. Here God remarks that His bride takes His corn and His wine and His oil and His silver and His gold to offer them to Baal; she uses the divine gifts in the service of evil! We have already explained the symbols of these gifts and their spiritual meanings in some detail.
As for the fruit of this painful conduct, it is:

First: God withdraws His gifts at the proper time, for He says: "Therefore will I return, and take away my corn in the time thereof, and my wine in the season thereof, and will recover my wool and my flax given to cover her nakedness" [9]. It is remarkable that God lets His bride do what she wishes with His gifts and talents, despite her misuse of them, that perhaps she may realize her error and return. But this leaving is for a time, for at the proper time He withdraws what He gave her, so she becomes hungry, thirsty and naked, exposed even before the eyes of her lovers. God is longsuffering toward us, but if we persist in misusing His gifts to us, He takes away what He gave us and makes us an example and a mockery even among the wicked, which the prophet Jeremiah realized when Jerusalem was taken captive, saying: "all that honoured her despise her, because they have seen her nakedness: yea, she sigheth, and turneth backward. Her filthiness is in her skirts... she had no comforter" (Lam 1:8-9).

Second: She loses not only the gifts and talents but also her joy and her temporal and eternal peace, for He says: "I will also cause all her mirth to cease, her feast days, her new moons, and her sabbaths, and all her solemn feasts" [11]. He causes all her temporal joys to cease, and she enters into perpetual bitterness, gloom and distress, and knows no more joy or feast. But the believer, in the midst of bearing the cross, has his heart drawn to the joy of the resurrection and its power, and in the midst of sufferings he tastes inner rest on a heavenly level, and in the midst of sorrow he rejoices and no one can take his joy from him.

St. John Chrysostom affirms in more than one place that man's peace and joy spring from his depths within through the holy life in the Lord, and that his harm does not spring from external factors but from his sin, for he says: [For this reason I do not fear the plots of enemies, but I fear one thing, sin; I want to teach you a lesson, which is not to fear the deceptions of the powerful, but fear the power of sin. No one harms you if you do not harm yourself by yourself. If you do not sin, tens of thousands of swords threaten you, but God snatches you from them so that they do not come near you; but if you commit evil, even if you are inside paradise you will be driven out of it.]

Third: He destroys her vines and her fig trees [12]; we saw earlier in the introduction to this commentary the vine and the fig tree as symbols of the suffering Church, marked by unity of spirit. It is as though the man who leaves the Bridegroom of his soul loses the traits of the Church and his membership in it, and even becomes a forest eaten by the beasts of the field [12], that is, prey for Satan and a table for sin.

Fourth: The end of all this is her receiving divine punishment, "And I will visit upon her the days of Baalim, wherein she burned incense to them, and she decked herself with her earrings and her jewels, and she went after her lovers, and forgat me, saith the LORD" [13]. God reckons with her exactly, because she offered incense to the idols of Baal and adorned herself for them with earrings and jewels and went after her lovers committing debauchery with them and left God, the fountain of holiness. She offered incense as a sign of prayer and refuge to Baal, and adorned herself for him as a sign of the desire to please him and be united with him, and ran after the lovers as an indication of the attachment of the heart. Thus she offered all her capacities to Baal and not to her Bridegroom, whom she had utterly forgotten, so she deserved to fall under eternal punishment.

14 "Therefore, behold, I will allure her, and bring her into the wilderness, and speak comfortably unto her. 15 And I will give her her vineyards from thence, and the valley of Achor for a door of hope: and she shall sing there, as in the days of her youth, and as in the day when she came up out of the land of Egypt. 16 And it shall be at that day, saith the LORD, that thou shalt call me my husband; and shalt call me no more Baali. 17 For I will take away the names of Baalim out of her mouth, and they shall no more be remembered by their name. 18 And in that day will I make a covenant for them with the beasts of the field, and with the fowls of heaven, and with the creeping things of the ground: and I will break the bow and the sword and the battle out of the earth, and will make them to lie down safely. 19 And I will betroth thee unto me for ever; yea, I will betroth thee unto me in righteousness, and in judgment, and in lovingkindness, and in mercies. 20 I will even betroth thee unto me in faithfulness: and thou shalt know the LORD. 21 And it shall come to pass in that day, I will hear, saith the LORD, I will hear the heavens, and they shall hear the earth; 22 And the earth shall hear the corn, and the wine, and the oil; and they shall hear Jezreel. 23 And I will sow her unto me in the earth; and I will have mercy upon Lo-ruhamah; and I will say to Lo-ammi, Thou art my people; and he shall say, Thou art my God."

After declaring the evil that the unfaithful bride committed and her squandering of her Bridegroom's wealth on behalf of His enemy, revealing the fruits of this vain conduct, He returns in tenderness and gentleness to declare His desire for her return to Him, for He says: "Therefore, behold, I will allure her, and bring her into the wilderness, and speak comfortably unto her" [14].

What bridegroom speaks tenderly to his bride after her betrayal of him and her squandering of his possessions on another? So God longs for man, allures him and speaks tenderly to him, that perhaps he may return to Him and accept union with Him. And since God sanctifies human freedom, He does not compel him to return, but allures him to draw him to Himself, to lead him into the wilderness, where he finds no helper but God alone, who speaks tenderly to him in the wilderness as He spoke tenderly to the people of Israel in the wilderness of Sinai, offering them all love and showing them all tenderness and care.

entries.section: And now, with what does God speak tenderly to her so that she may return to Him?

paragraphs.text: First: "I will give her her vineyards from thence" [15]; for although He takes her into the wilderness, He gives her her vineyards there in the wilderness, and vineyards provide food (grapes), drink (grape juice) and gladdening wine. What are these vineyards that the Lord gives her but Himself, for He says: "I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman" (Jn 15:1), as though He offers His life for satisfaction, refreshment and joy; she enjoys Him as the Bread that came down from heaven (Jn 6:50), and drinks from Him as the living fountain (Jer 2:13), and is made drunk with His love, saying: "Thy love is better than wine" (Song 1:2).

Although the world has become like a barren wilderness that cannot offer us anything, yet in the world we find the true vine come down to us that we may possess it, indeed that we may abide in it as branches and bring forth much fruit (Jn 15:5), and this is the secret of our joy and the exultation of our hearts in the midst of the wilderness of this world.

entries.section: And now, with what does God speak tenderly to her so that she may return to Him?

paragraphs.text: Second: "And I will give her... the valley of Achor for a door of hope: and she shall sing there, as in the days of her youth, and as in the day when she came up out of the land of Egypt" [15].

It is remarkable that when God takes her into the wilderness and offers Himself to her as "vineyards," she receives with the vineyards distress, for the word "Achor" means (trouble) or (affliction), and it is a valley in which Achar (Achan) the son of Zerah was stoned (Josh 7:26), about ten miles south of Jericho. He who receives the Lord Christ in the wilderness of this world receives Him as the satisfaction of his soul, but not without distress, and as St. John Chrysostom says, where Christ is, there also is the antichrist, resisting Him.

"Achor" is God's gift... "I will give her the valley of Achor," and as the Apostle Paul says of the gift of suffering: "For unto you it is given in the behalf of Christ, not only to believe on him, but also to suffer for his sake" (Phil 1:29), and as St. John Chrysostom says: [He lifts up our souls, counting these sufferings as His own; what joy fills us to be partakers with Christ, and to suffer for His sake!], [As He suffered from men, we too suffer with Him... therefore it is fitting for you not to be troubled by these sufferings but rather to rejoice in them.]

It is remarkable that God gives us "the valley of Achor for a door of hope," for in the midst of suffering the door of hope opens before us, as we taste the power of the resurrection and its joy through the cross with the Lord Christ, so we return to our renewed youth, and our tongue is opened in exultation, and our life is turned into an inner song of joy: "and she shall sing there, as in the days of her youth, and as in the day when she came up out of the land of Egypt" [15].

entries.section: And now, with what does God speak tenderly to her so that she may return to Him?

paragraphs.text: Third: She enjoys union with the heavenly Bridegroom: "And it shall be at that day, saith the LORD, that thou shalt call me my husband; and shalt call me no more Baali" [16], that is, she accepts union with God without using the pagan language (Baali, that is, my master or my lord); He sanctifies her completely even in her words, for He says: "For I will take away the names of Baalim out of her mouth, and they shall no more be remembered by their name."

entries.section: And now, with what does God speak tenderly to her so that she may return to Him?

paragraphs.text: She enters with Him into a marriage covenant that sanctifies her body and her mind and grants her surpassing peace even at her passing from this world. "And in that day will I make a covenant for them with the beasts of the field, and with the fowls of heaven, and with the creeping things of the ground: and I will break the bow and the sword and the battle out of the earth, and will make them to lie down safely" [18]. What is "that day" but the day of the coming of the Lord Christ and His being lifted up on the cross for our salvation, where He offered His shed blood as a new covenant, through which our sanctification is accomplished, so that the beasts of the field within us become tame, and the fowls of heaven, that is, the mind, become holy, and even the creeping things of the ground, that is, the lowest bodily energies, are blessed in Him, breaking by His cross the bow of sin and the sword of the devil and removing the battle from the body (the earth), as body and soul become sanctified in Him, and making even our lying down in the grave safe, where hell cannot seize us nor death corrupt our peace!

entries.section: And now, with what does God speak tenderly to her so that she may return to Him?

paragraphs.text: The secret of this divine work in our life is His saying, affirming it three times, "I will betroth thee unto me" [19-20], and He affirms "unto me," for God gives us Himself, and as St. John Chrysostom says to the Church in the words of the Lord Christ: [I promise you the Kingdom... yes, I have given you the greatest portion, I have given you even the Lord of the Kingdom!.

entries.section: As for the features of this heavenly betrothal, they are:

paragraphs.text: a. "I will betroth thee unto me for ever," an eternal betrothal that time cannot dissolve nor death corrupt... its foundation is the love that many waters cannot quench (Song 8:7)!

b. "I will betroth thee unto me in righteousness, and in judgment, and in lovingkindness, and in mercies" [19]. What are righteousness, judgment and love but the person of the Lord Christ, who came down to us so that mankind might enjoy the bride in Him! Through Him the Father came to us to carry us in His arms, and in Him we come before the Father as a bride for the only-begotten Son, having the right of sonship to Him and union with Him. By our union with the heavenly Bridegroom we bear His traits, that is, righteousness, judgment, lovingkindness and mercies, and we become heavenly, as St. John Chrysostom says: [Consider what the Spirit has done. He found the earth full of demons and made it heaven.]

entries.section: As for the features of this heavenly betrothal, they are:

paragraphs.text: c. "I will even betroth thee unto me in faithfulness: and thou shalt know the LORD" [20]. The foundation of the betrothal is faith, by which we are united with the Bridegroom, and He leads us to His Father and we come to know Him, not with the purely dry knowledge of the mind but with the knowledge of life and union, which the Lord Himself had earlier declared: "neither knoweth any man the Father, save the Son, and he to whom the Son will reveal him" (Mt 11:27). If union with Baal bears the fruit of ignorance of God, then union with the Son has as its aim entering into the Father's bosom and knowing Him closely and cleaving to Him!

entries.section: As for the features of this heavenly betrothal, they are:

paragraphs.text: Fourth: "And it shall come to pass in that day, I will hear, saith the LORD, I will hear the heavens, and they shall hear the earth" [21]. What are the heavens but the soul that bears the Lord Christ within it as its Bridegroom? The Father answers the soul united with the heavenly Bridegroom, for He smells in it the fragrance of good pleasure and it is the object of His delight. As for the earth, that is, the body, it is also sanctified with the soul and no longer resists God's work but becomes an instrument of righteousness working on His behalf; therefore the Lord hears this holy earth in which righteousness dwells. The earth no longer resists heaven, nor does the body wrestle with the holy soul, but responds to it and bears the fruits of the Spirit, which are from the sowing of God Himself: "And the earth shall hear the corn, and the wine, and the oil; and they shall hear Jezreel" [22].

entries.section: As for the features of this heavenly betrothal, they are:

paragraphs.text: Finally God concludes the blessings of this Messianic age, in which man returns to his Bridegroom, affirming the surpassing grace of God to us, saying: "And I will sow her unto me in the earth; and I will have mercy upon Lo-ruhamah; and I will say to Lo-ammi, Thou art my people; and he shall say, Thou art my God" [23]. God's own hand reaches out to sow us, so that we are no longer without mercy nor are we any longer not His people, but we enjoy His mercy and belonging to Him and take pride in His divinity.

"Jezreel" has become a promise after it was a threat, and has become a sign of God who sows His Church by Himself, after it was a sign of the vineyard seized by the wicked Jezebel. As for His promise: "I will have mercy upon Lo-ruhamah; and I will say to Lo-ammi, Thou art my people," the Apostle Paul quoted it in his Epistle to the Romans as a prophecy about the calling of the Gentiles, who were not pitied and not the people of God, saying: "As he saith also in Osee, I will call them my people, which were not my people; and her beloved, which was not beloved" (Rom 9:25).

1 Then said the LORD unto me, “Go yet, love a woman beloved of her friend, and an adulteress, according to the love of the LORD toward the children of Israel, who look to other gods and love cakes of raisins.”
Since scholars refuse to accept what is recorded here as a second marriage different from the one recorded in the first chapter, why did he repeat the event of marrying an adulteress?

First: some scholars hold that his wife Gomer the daughter of Diblaim fled from the marital home and sold herself to corruption, so that she became a slave, but the prophet returned and bought her for himself as a wife [2].

Second: some hold that what is recorded in this chapter is the very same thing that is recorded in the first chapter, but whereas the first chapter gave the command to marry, here he relates what actually happened, presenting to us the experience the prophet himself went through.

Third: a few scholars hold that the first account was directed to the northern kingdom (Israel), whereas here the account is directed to the southern kingdom (Judah), despite his saying “the children of Israel,” for the first kingdom was divorced and carried captive, and the second remained for a century and was also divorced and carried captive afterward.

Fourth: some hold that what is recorded here is merely a repetition of what is recorded in the first chapter, as an affirmation of God’s love for His fallen bride, and giving her more than one opportunity to reflect on the love of her first husband for her.

In the first chapter the Lord said to Hosea, “Go, take unto thee a wife of whoredoms,” but here He says to him, “love a woman beloved of her friend and an adulteress.” So the command came to him not merely to marry her as God’s command, but to love her despite his knowing that she was beloved of a friend and that she was an adulteress. Thus God wanted Hosea to enter into the fellowship of the love that God has toward His people, despite what this people had done, turning to other, pagan gods and eagerly taking part in corrupting feasts, for He says to him, “according to the love of the LORD toward the children of Israel, who look to other gods and love cakes of raisins” [1].
“So I bought her to me for fifteen shekels of silver, and for a homer and a lethech of barley” [2].

If this woman, in the desires of her heart, sold herself to the account of evil and became a lowly slave, so that her price became fifteen shekels of silver, that is, less than the price of a female slave; she ran after her lovers and offered her life as a vow to them, and so became worthless, for she lost her dignity and her glory, and lost the image in which her God had created her, who in His love had set her up in His image and likeness.

In any case, since Hosea is a type of Jesus Christ the Savior, his purchase of the adulterous woman points to His salvation of us, for He bought us with His precious blood from the bondage under whose yoke we ourselves had taken ourselves captive.
The prophet Hosea says, “I bought her to me.” Our Lord Jesus Christ acquired for Himself a bride who dedicates all her energies to His account, and not to the account of the world or Satan.

As for the price that Hosea paid, it was very paltry: fifteen shekels of silver, that is, less than the price of a male slave (Ex 21:22), and a homer and a lethech of barley and not wheat (Ps 81:16); the world valued her at barley, the food of the poor or of animals, and she deserved no more than this in its eyes. But our Lord Jesus acquired us not with gold or silver, nor with wheat or barley, but with His precious blood, as the Apostle says: “Knowing that ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold, from your vain conversation received by tradition from your fathers, but with the precious blood, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot, the blood of Christ” (1 Pet 1:18-19).

3 And I said unto her, “Thou shalt abide for me many days; thou shalt not play the harlot, and thou shalt not be for another man: so will I also be for thee.” 4 For the children of Israel shall abide many days without a king, and without a prince, and without a sacrifice, and without an image, and without an ephod and teraphim.

If God in His love runs after adulterous humanity, redeeming her with His blood, it is only in order to sanctify her and so prepare her for the heavenly wedding. For He says, “And I said unto her, ‘Thou shalt abide many days; thou shalt not play the harlot, and thou shalt not be for another man: so will I also be for thee’” [4]. The holy Son of God dedicated His work to the account of this wedding, saying, “so will I also be for thee,” and more clearly He says, “And for their sakes I sanctify myself, that they also might be sanctified through the truth” (Jn 17:19). The Holy One sanctified His life, that is, dedicated it to our salvation, so that we may be sanctified by Him, offering our lives to Him through sanctification by His blood by means of His Holy Spirit. And the wonder is that the soul’s spiritual marriage to God not only removes from her her uncleanness or spiritual adultery, but grants her “virginity.” As St. John Chrysostom says: [The Church is called a virgin, she who was formerly an adulteress. This is the miracle which the Bridegroom wrought: He took her as an adulteress and made her a virgin! What a wonderful and new thing! For through marriage we lose our virginity, but God through marriage restores her virginity to the Church… When you hear these things, do not understand them in a material way, but soar high in your thought. Do not understand them in a bodily way… for the Church which you live is spiritual, not material.]

The prophet continues his speech: “For the children of Israel shall abide many days without a king, and without a prince, and without a sacrifice, and without an image (an altar, according to the Septuagint), and without an ephod and teraphim” [4]. This is a reference to the period of captivity, in which the people were deprived of the freedom to worship God and all its privileges, and of every outward appearance of theirs as a nation or a church. Perhaps God permitted it as a period of preparation for them to receive true worship after they had been deprived of it because of their wickedness. God in His love deprives man even of blessings for a time, so that we may receive them in a greater and more lasting way!
5 Afterward shall the children of Israel return, and seek the LORD their God, and David their king; and shall run in fear to the LORD and to his goodness in the latter days.

He concludes the discourse on the acceptance of the adulteress into married love with the return of the Jewish people to the knowledge of God. Origen holds that the period of deprivation spoken of above does not refer only to the period of captivity, but also to the Jews’ rejection of the Messiah; yet in the last days they will accept the faith and join as members in the body of Christ to enjoy salvation, for he says: “Afterward shall the children of Israel return, and seek the LORD their God, and David their king; and shall run in fear to the LORD and to his goodness in the latter days” [5]. At the end of the ages they will run in fear to the Lord, or flee to Him.

Why does he say, “run in fear to the Lord”? Perhaps because they realize what sin did to David their king, that is, the Lord Christ, who is “the root and the offspring of David” (Rev 22:16), and they run in fear to Him to work out their salvation with fear and trembling (Phil 2:12).

1 Hear the word of the LORD, ye children of Israel: for the LORD hath a controversy with the inhabitants of the land, because there is no faithfulness, nor kindness, nor knowledge of God in the land. 2 Cursing, lying, killing, stealing, and committing adultery; they use violence, and blood toucheth blood. 3 Therefore shall the land mourn, and every one that dwelleth therein shall languish, with the beasts of the field and the fowls of heaven; yea, the fishes of the sea also shall be taken away.
God directs the accusation to the children of Israel, calling them the earth, or the inhabitants of the earth, and declaring the substance of the charge, saying:

“Hear the word of the LORD, ye children of Israel: for the LORD hath a controversy with the inhabitants of the land, because there is no faithfulness, nor kindness, nor knowledge of God in the land. Cursing, lying, killing, stealing, and committing adultery; they use violence, and blood toucheth blood” [2].
Since the children of Israel became attached to the love of earthly things, they became earth, and the substance of the charge is this:

First: from the negative side He says: “there is no faithfulness (in the Septuagint “truth”), nor kindness, nor knowledge of God in the land.” Israel came under trial as earth that had lost its union with the heavenly Bridegroom, because it carries within it neither truth, nor mercy, nor the knowledge of God. Without this inseparable trinity in his life, man descends to the transient earthly nature.

He begins with faithfulness or truth, as the Lord Christ says in His farewell prayer, “Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth” (Jn 17:17). They rejected the word of God and so rejected the truth, although it is not far from them: “The word is nigh thee, even in thy mouth, and in thy heart: that is, the word of faith, which we preach” (Rom 10:8). This truth must be joined to kindness or mercy, so that the word of God, or faith in it, is not merely memorized words or purely intellectual thought, but must touch our lives. And when the truth within us is turned into action, the “knowledge of God” increases in us and our insight is enlightened all the more. Thus truth interacts with action and knowledge, since they represent aspects intertwined together that belong to our life in Christ Jesus.

Second: since Israel lost this trinity of faith, action, and spiritual knowledge, it bore corruption: “Cursing, lying, killing, stealing; they use violence (they employ force), and blood toucheth blood.”

This list of sins declares at its beginning their breaking of the Ten Commandments (commandments 3, 9, 6, 8, 7), that is, the breaking of the covenant with God. As for his saying “they use violence,” it means the use of acts of violence contrary to the gentle Spirit of God. Perhaps it also means that they transgressed their bounds with God by violence, or that in their sins they transgress reason, conscience, or the Law not out of weakness or without will, but deliberately and violently. And by saying “blood toucheth blood,” he perhaps meant the blood of Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest, who was stoned in the court of the house of the LORD at the command of King Joash (2 Chr 24:21), so that his innocent blood was mingled with the blood of the sacrifices which they offered in a crooked spirit.

Third: he concludes his accusation of the children of Israel by saying: “Therefore shall the land mourn, and every one that dwelleth therein shall languish, with the beasts of the field and the fowls of heaven; yea, the fishes of the sea also shall be taken away” [3]. When Israel breaks God’s covenant it turns into a wilderness land that knows neither joy nor peace, but mourning and turmoil. There is no fruit in it, but famine and drought, and not even the wild animals, or the birds of heaven, or the fishes of the sea find food in it, but all languish. The fruit of breaking the covenant is a comprehensive ruin that touches the whole land with its animals, its birds, and its fishes.

He says, “the land shall mourn.” If the earth signifies the body for whose sake man commits evil to give it pleasure, then the fruit of this evil is the deprivation of this body of rest and joy, so that it remains mourning! This is the fruit of breaking the covenant with God, the Giver of peace, whereas union with Him gives man in his entirety true peace. As Fr. John of Kronstadt says: [When Christ dwells in the heart by faith, peace and joy dwell in it. For it is not without cause that God is said to be holy and to rest in His saints.] He also says: [I see with the eyes of my heart how I breathe in Christ in my heart with the mind, how He enters it and suddenly gives it peace and joy. Do not leave me to dwell alone without You, O Giver of life, my breath, my joy! For it is hard for me to be left without You.]

“And every one that dwelleth therein shall languish,” that is, man’s energies wither and his gifts are squandered, like the younger son who squandered his money in riotous living, so that he becomes like a dead man without worth, or a body without vitality. But the true believer praises truly, saying: “Thou visitest the earth, and makest it overflow; thou greatly enrichest it; the rivers of God are full of water… Thou blessest the fruits thereof. The pastures of the wilderness drop, and the little hills are girded with joy; the valleys are clothed with righteousness; they shout for joy, they also sing” (Ps 65:9, 13). It is as though he says to God: Even if I am dry earth, You tend me and make it overflow with goodness, sanctifying all Your gifts to me; You enrich it greatly, and fill my life with the waters of the Holy Spirit, who kindles all energies for the account of Your Kingdom; and You bless my inner produce, which is Your fruit in me, making my life fruitful and filled with joy and gladness, so that it speaks with praise and spiritual songs.

As for his saying: “with the beasts of the field and the fowls of heaven; yea, the fishes of the sea also shall be taken away,” in it there is a reference to the corruption of man’s life from every side: the land where the animals are, the air where the birds are, and the waters where the fishes are. The ruin has become so comprehensive that the wild animals, accustomed to the desolate wilderness, cannot live because of the severity of the drought, the birds of heaven find nothing to pick up, and even the fishes flee to other shores. Moreover, from another side, perhaps he wanted to reveal in his trial the gravity of sin, for it corrupts life, so that the ruin extends to the irrational creation of animals, birds, and fishes, as happened at the beginning of human life when the earth was cursed because of Adam and Eve and began to bring forth thorns and thistles. And from yet another side, perhaps the beasts of the field signify the bodily (animal) life, the fowls of heaven the thought, which it is fitting should soar in heavenly things, and the fishes of the sea the side of faith, as though man by leaving his heavenly Bridegroom shatters his life from all its sides, body, thought, and spirit, and loses all that he has.

4 “Yet let no one judge, and let no one rebuke. For thy people are as they that strive with the priest. 5 Therefore shalt thou stumble in the day, and the prophet also shall stumble with thee in the night, and I will destroy thy mother. 6 My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge: because thou hast rejected knowledge, I will also reject thee, that thou shalt be no priest to me: seeing thou hast forgotten the law of thy God, I will also forget thy children. 7 As they were increased, so they sinned against me: therefore will I change their glory into shame. 8 They eat up the sin of my people, and they lift up their souls to their iniquity. 9 And there shall be, like people, like priest: and I will punish them for their ways, and reward them their doings. 10 For they shall eat, and not have enough: they shall commit whoredom, and shall not increase: because they have left the service of the LORD.”

Having announced His trial of all the children of Israel and presented the substance of the charge, He called for the trial of the priests, together with the false prophets, as those first responsible for what this people had come to.

He says: “Yet let no one judge (other than him), and let no one rebuke. For thy people are as they that strive with the priest. Therefore shalt thou stumble in the day, and the prophet also shall stumble with thee in the night, and I will destroy thy mother” [5]. Perhaps he means here that every person is responsible for himself, and no one may justify the priest’s conduct merely because he is a priest, for since he stumbles by day, and with him the false prophets stumble by night through vain dreams, all share in the ruin of Samaria, the capital of Israel, their mother. It is as though the wicked priests had united with the false prophets in stumbling by day and by night, shattering the whole people.

Some hold that the address here is directed to the people, where God asks that the sincere reprovers be silent and withdraw from this work, because there is no one who listens to the voice of reproof, so that they have become so hardened that they reject all guidance even if a priest offers it. They strive with the priest who is frank with them, and even persecute him, as Joash king of Judah and his people did when they stoned Zechariah the son of Jehoiada in the court of the house of the LORD because he spoke the words of the LORD (2 Chr 24:21).

God directs His speech to the priests, declaring that they destroyed the people through lack of knowledge: “My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge: because thou hast rejected knowledge, I will also reject thee, that thou shalt be no priest to me” [6]. We have already clarified in the introduction to the book what is meant by the knowledge of God in this book, and we saw the link between the knowledge of God and the godly life made holy in the Lord. The priests left the life of fellowship with God and busied themselves with their own interests, so they lost godly knowledge and became like those who are in the darkness of ignorance. He did not say, “because thou art ignorant,” but “because thou hast rejected knowledge”; as though He says to him: You are without excuse, for knowledge is available to you and the light is present, but you reject knowledge and do not accept the light, as it is said: “they have no delight in the knowledge of the ways of God” (Job 21:14). The secret of their rejection of knowledge is their abandoning of the word of God or the commandment: “seeing thou hast forgotten the law of thy God, I will also forget thy children” [6]. Thus He links the knowledge of God with the law of God, since the latter is its source. As Fr. John of Kronstadt says: [Holy Scripture is the center of God’s wisdom, His word, and His Spirit… In it He declares of Himself: “The words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life” (Jn 6:63). In Holy Scripture we see God face to face, and we see ourselves as we are, so that man knows himself through it, and walks always in the presence of God.]

And if we take the symbolic meaning, who is the priest who rejects the knowledge of God so that all the people perish, and forgets the law of God so that God forgets his children, if not the heart, which ought to have been the center of the Kingdom of God, yet is attached to the world and temporal things, and so loses its purity and does not see God, but becomes like one in spiritual blindness without living knowledge, forgetting the commandment or pretending to forget it. This heart that rejects knowledge through purity destroys all the people, that is, the whole body with its energies and capacities, and when it forgets the divine commandment the commandment bears no fruit in it, so that it is like one who has forgotten her children.

By this we understand what we have said before, that knowledge is not acquired through reading alone but through the godly life of devotion made holy in the Lord, through the inner priest, that is, the pure heart which intercedes for the whole body before God.

The Lord continues His rebuke of the priests, saying: “As they were increased, so they sinned against me: therefore will I change their glory into shame. They eat up the sin of my people, and they lift up their souls to their iniquity. And there shall be, like people, like priest: and I will punish them for their ways, and reward them their doings. For they shall eat, and not have enough: they shall commit whoredom, and shall not increase: because they have left the service of the LORD” [7-10]. They relied on the multitude of their number or the quantity of work and not on its quality, therefore “as they were increased, so they sinned against me”; instead of their inner sanctification and their true witness before the people of God, they became all the more sinners against God. They were occupied with pagan feasts and fell into abominations, therefore they were condemned together with the people without partiality.

“They eat up the sin of my people,” that is, they eat the sin offerings which the people present, so they are not concerned with the people’s repentance and their turning back from evil, but rejoice in the people’s offering of sacrifices for the sake of their own enjoyment of the sacrifices, for the more the people sinned, the more their portion increased through the abundance of sacrifices! They were concerned not with repentance but with filling their bellies with meat at the expense of the people’s sanctification. Therefore they eat and are not satisfied, and commit adultery by taking concubines, so the blessing is removed from them. It is a hideous picture unbecoming of a priest, therefore Fr. John of Kronstadt warns us, saying: [The priest is an angel, not a man, and it is fitting for him to cast every worldly matter far behind him. O Lord, may Your priests be clothed with righteousness (Ps 132:9). May they remember always the greatness of their calling, and not fall into the snares of the world and Satan, but be delivered from the cares of the world, the deceitfulness of riches, and the lusts of all other things that enter their hearts (Mk 4:19).]

11 “Whoredom and wine and new wine take away the heart. 12 My people ask counsel at their stocks, and their staff declareth unto them: for the spirit of whoredoms hath caused them to err, and they have gone a whoring from under their God. 13 They sacrifice upon the tops of the mountains, and burn incense upon the hills, under oaks and poplars and elms, because the shadow thereof is good! Therefore your daughters shall commit whoredom, and your daughters-in-law shall commit adultery. 14 I will not punish your daughters when they commit whoredom, nor your daughters-in-law when they commit adultery: for themselves are separated with whores, and they sacrifice with those who vow whoredom: and the people that doth not understand shall be overthrown. 15 Though thou, Israel, play the harlot, yet let not Judah offend; and come not ye unto Gilgal, neither go ye up to Beth-aven, nor swear, The LORD liveth. 16 For Israel slideth back as a backsliding heifer: now the LORD will feed them as a lamb in a large place. 17 Ephraim is joined to idols: let him alone. 18 When their carousing is ended, they commit whoredom upon whoredom. Her shields love, they love disgrace. 19 The wind hath bound her up in her wings, and they shall be ashamed because of their sacrifices.”
After announcing His trial of all the children of Israel, especially the religious leaders, He reveals the abominations into which all had fallen:

First: “Whoredom and wine and new wine take away the heart” [11]. Their turning from the worship of God to the worship of Baal was caused by bodily pleasures, and as St. Augustine says, behind every atheism there is a lust. For the lusts of the flesh, if left without restraint, corrupt the heart and kill in it every longing for God as the Bridegroom of the soul, so man resorts to fleeing from God, regarding Him as one who stifles his breath and shatters his personality.

Second: when man gives himself over to the enjoyment of bodily pleasures without restraint, he descends to improper and unacceptable conduct such as acts of sorcery, which were at that time linked with the worship of Baal. God says: “My people ask counsel at their stocks (perhaps the wooden statue of Baal), and their staff declareth unto them.” Instead of turning to the Lord their God and asking Him for counsel, they began to resort to the statue of Baal and acts of sorcery to determine their way for them and reveal the future to them. Everyone who leaves the word of God and resorts to the world and to men is like one who consults the wood and asks the staff.

Third: their rush into pagan worship; they offer sacrifices on the tops of the mountains and incense on the hills, and under the oaks, the poplars, and the elms, because the shadow thereof is good [13]. Israel encompassed mountains that ought to have been holy (Jer 31:23), to which those who desire salvation flee (Gen 19:17), upon which the heavenly Bridegroom comes leaping (Song 2:8), upon which the city of Jerusalem is built (Mt 5:14), so that it cannot be hid, to which the Lord Christ went up (Jn 6:3), and which drop down spiritual new wine unceasingly (Joel 3:18). These mighty mountains were turned to the account of the devil, and defiled altars were set up upon them.

And as Israel encompassed mighty mountains that were turned to the account of Baal, so it also encompassed smaller souls, which are the hills upon which the Lord Christ ought to have come leaping (Song 2:8); these too were corrupted and carried the smell of defiled incense.
What I say of the mountains and hills I repeat of the oaks, the poplars, and the elms, which, instead of glorifying God, became centers for the account of the kingdom of darkness.

In any case, the Jews chose the high places such as mountain summits and hilltops, not in order to rise by them in thought above earthly things, but to think that they had drawn near to heaven, and behold, they sank down to the abyss. And they chose the thick trees, thinking that they would help them in spiritual contemplation, instead of resorting to the shadow of the Cross and resting in the pierced side.
Finally He presents to us a hideous picture of the spread of adultery in their life, giving us the features of their defiled life, which are:

A. This sin was committed by unmarried daughters and by married daughters-in-law (the wives of the sons). It was as though the sin had become general, characterizing the female sex, so that the unmarried girl is not ashamed to commit it, nor is the married daughter-in-law ashamed of it.

B. It is as though God had despaired of them, for they committed the sin not out of weakness, nor in the midst of their striving, but were doing evil continually, without shame and by their own will; therefore God refuses to discipline them, and this is a punishment under which man falls, to be deprived of God’s fatherhood through God’s refraining from disciplining him, for He says: “I will not punish your daughters when they commit whoredom, nor your daughters-in-law when they commit adultery” [14]. As Fr. Theodore says: [He is like a skilled physician who has used every means of treatment and there is no remedy left that can be used. God was overcome by their injustice and was compelled to cease His gentle disciplines, exposing them, saying: “So will I make my fury toward thee to rest, and my jealousy shall depart from thee, and I will be quiet, and will be no more angry” (Ezek 16:42).] And St. Jerome says: [Blessed is the man who is disciplined in this life, for God does not discipline twice for one thing [(Nah 1:9) Septuagint]. How great is the wrath of the Lord when He is not angry with us here, for by this He keeps us like an ox for the slaughter. In truth He says to Jerusalem that her sins are many and her evils great, therefore His jealousy departs from her and He is no more angry with her (Ezek 16:42). In other words He says: “When you were merely an adulteress I loved you and was jealous over you, but when you had many lovers I despised you, so I am not jealous and no more angry.” In the same sense, when a man loves his wife he is jealous over her, but when he hates her he does not say with God, “I will visit their transgression with the rod” (Ps 89:34), but says: “I will not punish your daughters when they commit whoredom” (v. 14).]

C. What the daughters and women do is the natural fruit of the hideousness of what the men do, as He says: “for themselves are separated with whores, and they sacrifice with those who vow whoredom, and the people that doth not understand shall be overthrown” [14]. If the men and young men go to the altars of Baal scattered throughout all the land and are separated with harlots, offering sacrifices of evil with the priestesses who vow their lives to corruption for the account of Baal, then these men conduct themselves without understanding and are overthrown before defilement, or fall under sin; therefore God gave over their wives and their daughters to these lusts, for He says: “Therefore your daughters shall commit whoredom, and your daughters-in-law shall commit adultery” [13]. Thus God bitterly disciplines adulterers so that they may realize the hideousness of their conduct, as He formerly punished David by the defiling of his concubines (2 Sam 2:11).

D. He describes them in their commission of this evil as the backsliding heifer [16] that does not accept the yoke, and when it is put upon her she balks to resist and goes back instead of walking forward with it to fulfill the purpose of her owner. Thus this people rejected the yoke of God’s commandment, and wanted to run madly after their own desire and not according to the will of God, and they went backward instead of advancing forward.

They set out for the places where adultery and pagan worship had spread, such as Gilgal and Beth-aven (the house of vanity), and so became like the lamb that feeds in a large place to be prepared for slaughter: “they grow fat and kick” (Deut 32:15).

E. He says: “Ephraim is joined to idols: let him alone” [17], and in the Septuagint: “Ephraim is joined (or a partner) to idols, he places stumbling blocks for himself in his way.” He bound himself by himself to the idols, and so became a partner to them, bearing their traits in himself. Since they are of stone, his heart became of stone, and since they are transient and vain, he gave himself over to destruction and vanity.

Ephraim was joined to the idols and so became as one bound to them and enslaved to them, unable to hear good counsel or to be freed from them. This is the nature of sin, as St. Anba Antony the Great says: [When the soul is ignorant of sin, sin is beloved to it, and even enslaves the soul that loves it and takes it captive.]

F. Finally He asks: what becomes of their carousing?! Or what will be the end of this bitter drink? “Her shields love, they love disgrace.
