The wind hath bound her up in her wings, and they shall be ashamed because of their sacrifices” [18-19]. They loved disgrace, that is, shameful gain and corruption, and received shame. And finally the raging wind carries them off into captivity, as on wings of evil, to bring them into the humiliation of bondage, and then they will be ashamed of their pagan sacrifices which could not save them.

If this people lived for a time in the spirit of the Gentiles, worshiping idols, then they will receive the desire of their heart when they are carried off as captives to where pagan worship is and to deprivation of Jerusalem and the temple of the Lord, and so taste the bitterness of the fruit of their work!

1 “Hear ye this, O priests! and hearken, ye house of Israel! and give ye ear, O house of the king! for judgment is toward you, because ye have been a snare on Mizpah, and a net spread upon Tabor. 2 And they have gone deep into the sacrifices of deviation, and I am a chastisement to them all. 3 I know Ephraim, and Israel is not hid from me: for now, O Ephraim, thou committest whoredom, and Israel is defiled. 4 Their doings will not suffer them to turn unto their God: for the spirit of whoredoms is in the midst of them, and they have not known the LORD. 5 And the pride of Israel is humbled in his face: therefore shall Israel and Ephraim fall in their iniquity; Judah also shall fall with them.”

God affirms that He shows no partiality to one group at the expense of another, or to one person at the expense of another, but since all have sinned He disciplines all, saying: “I am a chastisement to them all” [2]. He disciplines Israel because it began the evil and set up for itself a temple other than the temple of the Lord in Jerusalem and turned aside to idolatry; and at the same time He also disciplines Judah, despite the privileges it bore, since its capital is Jerusalem and within it is the temple of the Lord, and it is a royal tribe, but since it sinned, even if late, it is punished: “therefore shall Israel and Ephraim fall in their iniquity; Judah also shall fall with them” [5].

If in the previous chapter a trial was announced particularly against the priests, since the people of God perished through lack of knowledge, a matter which is at the very heart of the priests’ responsibility, yet this does not excuse the people, for He says: “Hear ye this, O priests! and hearken, ye house of Israel!” [1], and He includes with them the people of dignities: “and give ye ear, O house of the king! for judgment is toward you” [1].

He condemns all, for He is the Searcher of all and nothing is hidden from Him: “I know Ephraim, and Israel is not hid from me” [3]. He mentioned Ephraim first either in the sense of the kingdom of Israel, or because Ephraim was the chief of the rebels and through him the rest of the ten tribes were defiled; therefore he mentioned him first, since he deserves discipline more than others.
What does God know about them?

First: “ye have been a snare on Mizpah, and a net spread upon Tabor” [1]. Perhaps he addresses here the leaders who ought to have supported the weak lest they fall, and behold, they became snares and nets which the enemy sets to catch every soul for the account of evil. Instead of guiding them to repentance they entice them to fall and draw them by every device to pagan worship. Some think that it was their custom to station spies on the roads, especially on the two mountains “Mizpah and Tabor,” in the days of the feasts, to watch those going to Jerusalem and report on them so that they might be tried.

It is not known whether he means here the Mizpah which is in Gilead (Judg 11:21), which is said to be the place of the heap of stones which Jacob and the people of Laban set up as a witness to the covenant made between them (Gen 31:49), and there the children of Israel gathered to fight the Ammonites (Judg 10:17), and Jephthah met his daughter (Judg 11:34), and perhaps its location was Tell Ramith; or whether it is the Mizpah which is in Benjamin where Saul was chosen king (1 Sam 10:17, 21), and which Asa fortified (1 Kgs 15:22), and where Gedaliah was killed (2 Kgs 25:23, 25), and it is said that it was the village of the prophet Samuel. In any case Mizpah and Mount Tabor were at that time two important centers of pagan worship, and they became symbols of the ruin that came because of pagan worship.

Second: their insistence on committing sin without repentance, because it springs from their depths, and because of their not knowing the Lord. “Their doings will not suffer them to turn unto their God: for the spirit of whoredoms is within them (in the midst of them), and they have not known the LORD” [4]. They are stubborn, insisting on turning away from God in ignorance.

Third: their haughtiness, or the pride of their heart, makes them despise the words of the Lord on the lips of the prophets, for He says: “And the pride of Israel is humbled in his face” [5]. “Indeed pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall. Better it is to be of an humble spirit with the meek, than to divide the spoil with the proud” (Prov 16:18-19). The Lord declared His hatred of man’s pride: “The Lord GOD hath sworn by himself, saith the LORD the God of hosts, I abhor the excellency of Jacob, and hate his palaces: therefore will I deliver up the city with all that is therein” (Amos 6:8). And He says: “Thus will I mar the pride of Judah, and the great pride of Jerusalem. This people, which refuse to hear my words, which walk in the stubbornness of their heart” (Jer 13:9-10).

6 “They shall go with their flocks and with their herds to seek the LORD; but they shall not find him; he hath withdrawn himself from them. 7 They have dealt treacherously against the LORD: for they have begotten strange children: now shall a month devour them with their portions.”

In the pride of their hearts and their ignorance they thought they could appease God with material offerings and sacrifices without changing their hearts; therefore He says: “They shall go with their flocks and with their herds to seek the LORD; but they shall not find him; he hath withdrawn himself from them” [6]. The secret of His withdrawing from them is that they approach Him but not with their heart, therefore they do not find Him, for He is found only by the heart and seen only by it: “Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God” (Mt 5:8).

If He withdrew from them, it is because they dealt treacherously with Him, they broke the covenant made between Him and them, and instead of being united to Him to bring forth the fruit of the Spirit that gladdens the heart of God, they were united to evil and brought forth strange children, that is, fruits foreign to God… “They have dealt treacherously against the LORD: for they have begotten strange children” [7].

He concludes his saying thus: “now shall a month devour them with their portions” [7]. Perhaps he meant that at the monthly feast (the new moon), instead of rejoicing and being glad in the Lord and being satisfied with the spiritual fruit as the Lord rejoices in them, behold, they practice the ritual of the feast, but in it they lose everything, even their possessions (their portions); and perhaps by their portions which they lose he meant the defiled tables which they set up in celebration of Baal, for these became their portion instead of God Himself and His Kingdom being their portion, and this portion which they chose they lose because it is transient.

entries.section: 3. Announcement of a general state of discipline

paragraphs.text: 8 “Blow ye the trumpet in Gibeah, the horn in Ramah. Cry aloud at Beth-aven: after thee, O Benjamin. 9 Ephraim shall be desolate in the day of chastisement. Among the tribes of Israel have I made known that which is sure. 10 The princes of Judah are like them that remove the bound: therefore I will pour out my wrath upon them like water. 11 Ephraim is oppressed, crushed in judgment, because he willingly walked after the commandment. 12 Therefore am I unto Ephraim as a moth, and to the house of Judah as the woodworm.”

God asks for the blowing of trumpets in both kingdoms, Israel and Judah, which are used in wars; as though God wanted to declare to them what sin does to them, for it makes the God who loves mankind appear as an enemy of theirs who fights them. In any case He asked for the blowing of the trumpets in Gibeah and the horn in Ramah, and He asked them to cry aloud at Beth-aven.

“Gibeah” means (hill), and the horn signifies power, while Ramah means (high place), as though God asks for the blowing of the trumpets on the hill in a very high place where they think they are strong, so that they may realize they are in a state of war… They accepted pagan worship and so entered into enmity with God, and behold, He permits them to be disciplined through the raids of enemies, worshipers of Baal, who attack them and plunder them of everything and take them captive. They loved Baal and his feasts and pleasures, so let them accept slavery to the people of Baal and the worshipers of strangers!

It is said that Gibeah is very close to Ramah, the first on the border of the kingdom of Judah, and the second in Israel, as though ruin comes upon both kingdoms because both have been corrupted. As for “Beth-aven” or (house of vanity)… there is no need to blow the trumpet in it, for it has utterly declined and fallen without hope, and nothing is heard in it but cries of defeat since the enemy has seized it.

He continues his speech: “after thee, O Benjamin” [8], and in some translations “Be terrified, O Benjamin.” Since the enemy has seized the hill country of Ephraim and come very near the border of Benjamin, there is no need to blow the trumpet in Benjamin, but it is enough to look behind to make souls tremble, and let them repent and return to the Lord so that what befell Ephraim may not befall them.

entries.section: 3. Announcement of a general state of discipline

paragraphs.text: He continues his speech: “Among the tribes of Israel have I made known that which is sure. The princes of Judah are like them that remove the bound: therefore I will pour out my wrath upon them like water” [9-10]. God has declared in the kingdom of Israel what is sure, that is, the certain discipline that must come upon them, and not, as they thought, mere threats without action. As for the princes of Judah, God pours out upon them and the kingdom of Baal. They lost the spirit of discernment, “who distinguishes between the Egyptians (symbolically),” for nothing grieves the heart of God like the spiritual leaders’ losing the spirit of discernment, the spirit which every believer ought to carry within him.

Perhaps removing the bound also means seizure or greed; therefore the commandment came: “Thou shalt not remove thy neighbour’s landmark, which they of old time have set in thine inheritance, which thou shalt inherit in the land that the LORD thy God giveth thee to possess it” (Deut 19:14), so that a tribe may not go beyond the borders of its land but keep to the borders that God gave it.

entries.section: 3. Announcement of a general state of discipline

paragraphs.text: “Ephraim is oppressed (under pressure), crushed in judgment, because he willingly walked after the commandment. Therefore am I unto Ephraim as a moth, and to the house of Judah as the woodworm” [11-12].

Ephraim fell under pressure until he was utterly crushed, so that there was no breath of life left in him; he also lost his strength, his privileges, and his rights because he agreed to walk after the commandment of Jeroboam, and of the kings after him, who compelled their subjects to the vain worship of Baal. Therefore the word “commandment” came in the Septuagint as “vanity,” that is, Ephraim agreed to walk after vanity instead of the commandment of God, which is the truth. This conduct causes them to lose the enjoyment of God’s blessings in their lives, and God becomes to them like the moth that spoils the garment, so that their nakedness and shame are exposed, and God will be to Judah also like the woodworm that destroys wood or the beams of a house, so that the house collapses and Judah is left without shelter.

13 “When Ephraim saw his sickness, and Judah saw his wound, then went Ephraim to Assyria, and sent to an enemy king: yet could he not heal you, nor cure you of your wound. 14 For I will be unto Ephraim as a lion, and as a young lion to the house of Judah: I, even I, will tear and go away; I will take away, and none shall rescue him. 15 I will go and return to my place, till they are requited and seek my face: in their affliction they will seek me early.”

These general disciplines revealed the sickness of Israel and the wounds of Judah, and it was fitting for them to turn to God in repentance, but Israel resorted to Assyria to support it [13], and behold, Assyria and its men were “miserable comforters” (Job 16:2) and “physicians of no value” (Job 13:4), and instead of supporting them they distressed them (2 Chr 28:16, 18). And since Israel did not benefit from the discipline, it came under a harsher and more bitter discipline, so we do not see God toward it as the moth or the woodworm but as the lion and the young lion. And in all this God hopes for its return: “I, even I, will tear and go away; I will take away, and none shall rescue him. I will go and return to my place, till they pass over and seek my face: in their affliction they will seek me early” [14-15].

What does He mean by saying, “I will return to my place”? Perhaps He wanted to make clear that in moments of discipline or the punishment of the wicked He is like one who “cometh out of his place” (Isa 26:21), appearing as one who is harsh, while His return to His place means His longing to declare His love for them and His accompaniment of them.

Finally, affliction makes the soul seek God early, therefore the Apostle advises us: “Is any among you afflicted? let him pray” (Jas 5:13). As Fr. John of Kronstadt says: [Often we draw near to God in time of distress, when no one but God can deliver us from it, and we return to Him with all our hearts… whereas in times of ease and abundance we leave God, especially when man thirsts for wealth and glory and distinction above others, for when he obtains these things he loses his faith from his heart and forgets God his Judge who will recompense him, forgets the immortality of his soul and his obligation to love God with all his heart and his neighbor as himself.]

1 Come, and let us return unto the LORD: for he hath torn, and he will heal us; he hath smitten, and he will bind us up. 2 After two days will he revive us: in the third day he will raise us up, and we shall live in his sight. 3 Let us know, let us follow on to know the LORD. His going forth is sure as the morning; and he shall come unto us as the rain, as the latter rain that watereth the earth.

When God tightens the noose on His fallen children, they seek Him early (Hos 5:15), saying: “Come, and let us return unto the LORD: for he hath torn, and he will heal us; he hath smitten, and he will bind us up” [1]. If He is like a lion that tears, it is only to heal us; if He smites, it is only to bind up our brokenness. As St. John Chrysostom wrote to a young widow wounded by the death of her husband at the hand of God, who permitted her this trial, saying: [Now I offer you this letter to be the first and greatest witness of God’s care for you, so that grief may not swallow you up, and your natural thoughts may not tear you down, when these troubles suddenly work to distress you… For it is said, “he hath torn, and he will heal us” [2], “he will smite us and bind up our wounds and heal us”… Now God has taken your husband to Himself, so He takes his place for you!] If His hand firmly holds the scalpel to wound, it is in truth uncovering our depths that bear the smell of death and corruption, and His hand remains stretched out to dress the wounds and grant us resurrection from the death in which we are; therefore He says: “After two days will he revive us: in the third day he will raise us up, and we shall live with him” [2].

He had said before: “in their affliction they will seek me early” (Hos 5:15), as though they stand early before the Lord Christ risen from the dead to find in His resurrection their own resurrection from among the dead. Truly it is fitting for us to enter with Him into His holy tomb, and to be buried with Him for “two days,” so that He may raise us on the third day and we may live before Him bearing His traits in us. We no longer fear the tomb as long as we are members of the body of the Lord Christ, which will not see corruption and which death cannot hold.

Thus the prophet saw, more than 700 years before the coming of the Lord Christ, in the resurrection of the Lord from the dead the secret of spiritual power… “we shall rise with him,” “we shall live with him,” “we shall know the Lord” [1-2]. By His resurrection we enjoy the good life that has become ours in Him, that is, the heavenly, exalted life, and by this we come to know the Lord. It is as though we enjoy what the two disciples of Emmaus obtained, those whom the Lord Christ, risen from the dead, accompanied, and as He spoke with them their hearts burned within them with His love and their inner sight was opened and they knew Him, saying to one another: “Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures?” (Lk 24:32).

Hosea, in the spirit of prophecy, presented to us the time of His resurrection, namely the dawn of the third day, for he says: “in the third day he will raise us up… His going forth is sure as the morning” [3]. The Church has been accustomed since the apostolic age to remember His resurrection constantly, especially in the Prime prayer, at dawn, the time of His resurrection, and as St. Cyprian says: [We must also pray in the morning, so that we celebrate by it the resurrection of the Lord]
The Lord rose at the dawn of the third day, to raise us at the dawn of our spiritual life; when we seek Him in us, He declares the power of His resurrection in our lives continually.

Perhaps his saying, “His going forth is sure as the morning,” means the certainty and assurance of His going forth, dispelling the darkness. The Septuagint reads: “we shall find him ready as the morning,” and as St. Augustine says, God is always present even if we do not perceive Him, “He was in the world, and the world was made by him, and the world knew him not” (Jn 1:10); when we return to Him He returns to us (Zech 1:3). And as St. John Chrysostom says: [The prophet points to the constant readiness of His goodness… for when we draw near to Him we find Him awaiting our movement.]

After announcing the resurrection of the Lord at the dawn of the third day, the secret of our salvation, he presents to us the work of the Holy Spirit, who was given to us later, “in the fullness of time,” after the ascension of the Lord Christ, for he says: “and he shall come unto us as the rain, as the latter rain that watereth the earth.” His Holy Spirit comes to us, descending upon us like the rain to transform us from dryness into a joyful garden, bearing the fruit of the Spirit that gladdens the heart of the Father, and the soul hears the whisper of her Bridegroom to her: “A garden inclosed is my sister, my spouse” (Song 4:12).

St. Hippolytus of Rome sees in this rain a reference to the Lord Christ Himself, for he speaks in a discourse on the Holy Theophany (the Epiphany) of the dignity of the waters into which the Lord Christ entered and with which He was covered: [As for the water, there is something greater than all, namely the fact that Christ the Creator of all came down like the rain (Hos 6:3), and was known as the fountain (Jn 4:14), and was poured out as a river (Jn 7:38), and was baptized in the Jordan (Mt 3:13)… How wonderful that He is immersed in a little water, He who is the boundless river (Ps 46:4) which makes glad the city of God! The unfailing fountain, who bears life for all mankind, is covered by poor and temporary waters, He who is without end! He who is present in every place and is not absent from any place, whom the angels cannot comprehend and whom men cannot look upon, comes to Baptism according to His good pleasure.]

4 “O Ephraim, what shall I do unto thee? O Judah, what shall I do unto thee? for your goodness is as a morning cloud, and as the early dew it goeth away. 5 Therefore have I hewed them by the prophets; I have slain them by the words of my mouth: and the judgment upon thee is as the light that goeth forth. 6 For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings. 7 But they like Adam have transgressed the covenant: there have they dealt treacherously against me. 8 Gilead is a city of them that work iniquity, and is trodden with blood. 9 And as troops of robbers wait for a man, so the company of priests murder in the way toward Shechem: for they have committed lewdness. 10 I have seen an horrible thing in the house of Israel: there is the whoredom of Ephraim, Israel is defiled. 11 Also, O Judah, he hath set an harvest for thee, when I returned the captivity of my people.”

God Himself is the Savior; He rises from the dead to raise us with Him, and gives us His Holy Spirit as a latter rain that removes our dryness, giving His fruits in us, and not from ourselves. Therefore He says: “O Ephraim, what shall I do unto thee? O Judah, what shall I do unto thee? for your goodness (your righteousness) is as a morning cloud, and as the early dew it goeth away” [4]. Ephraim and Judah forgot their God and thought they were able to attain righteousness or goodness by their own work, and behold, this righteousness is like the morning cloud or the dew, unable to stand before the sun of trials. It is as though God says to them: What shall I do to you? For my part I have offered you my resurrection as the secret of your resurrection and given you my Holy Spirit to water your hearts, so why do you deprive yourselves of these my gifts, relying on your own righteousness, which is like the morning cloud and like the dew that quickly passes away?! And as St. John Chrysostom declares on the lips of the Lord: [He means this: for my part I offered everything indeed, but the hot sun comes upon you and scatters the cloud and the dew and makes them as nothing; therefore it is your evil that deprives you of my unspeakable goodness.]

The Lord continues His speech with them: “Therefore have I hewed them by the prophets; I have slain them by the words of my mouth: and the judges upon thee are as the light that goeth forth” [5]. And in the Septuagint: “Therefore I will reap (cut) your prophets, I will slay them by the words of my mouth…” They leaned on the false prophets who quieted their consciences with sweet, false words; therefore God disciplines these wicked men, and His judgment is like a slayer to them and like a light that exposes their darkness. As it is said: “he shall smite the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips shall he slay the wicked” (Isa 11:4).

If the words of God are life-giving, they are also deadly to evil and death, for the Lord by His words removes the deceit that is in the heart and kills it, shattering every darkness within us so that His judgment may appear as light in us. He is the one who shatters evil to build virtue, and scatters darkness so as to shine with His light in us.

Man cannot bring about inner reform of the heart… He can indeed offer sacrifices and burnt offerings and gifts and outward shows of devotion, but who is it that gives mercy and love and the knowledge of God and faithfulness in the covenant?! Therefore He says: “For I desired mercy (steadfast love), and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings. But they like Adam have transgressed the covenant: there have they dealt treacherously against me” [6-7]. He wants inner works and a change of heart, which they cannot do from themselves, but it is the work of God Himself.

God is the one who works in us to grant us “mercy” or “steadfast love” in us, which gladdens His heart. The message of the Lord Christ came focusing on offering a change of our hard nature into the likeness of His nature, full of tenderness and love, so that we bear His traits in us.

St. John Chrysostom speaks to us about this mercy that God seeks in us, saying: [Now is not the time for judgment but for mercy; it is not for us to demand an account but to show love, it is not for us to bring suits but to waive them; it is not a time for judging and revenge, but to show mercy and do good.] This mercy is the nature of God Himself, as St. Ambrose writes in his treatise “On Repentance” against the followers of Novatian, who close the doors of God’s mercies before those who commit certain sins, saying: [We must know that God is a God of mercy, inclined to pardon and not to harshness. Therefore it is said: “I desire mercy, and not sacrifice.” How then does God accept your gifts, you who deny mercy, when it has been said of God that He has no pleasure in the death of the sinner, as that he should return (Ezek 18:32)?]

Through this divine mercy which we bear within us we come to know God, a knowledge of sharing His traits, which is what the Lord wants in us… “I desire… the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.” By this we bear within us faithfulness to the covenant made between God and us, and we are not counted as transgressors of it and traitors to it.

Let our reform be divine within, so that it may not be said of us: “But they like Adam have transgressed the covenant: there have they dealt treacherously against me. Gilead is a city of them that work iniquity, and is trodden with blood” [8]. May we not be like Adam, who transgressed the divine covenant while in the Paradise which God had set up for him, and so was counted a traitor to his Creator; may we enjoy His gifts and not deny His person. May we not be like Gilead, the city of them that work iniquity, trodden with blood, which is most likely the city of Ramoth-gilead, one of the three cities of refuge across the Jordan, a city of the Levites, containing men of the holy tribe, yet they were doers of evil who defiled themselves with blood through injustice and corruption. They had the appearance of piety and worship as Levites while in their depths they were wicked. May we also not be like the company of priests who put on the splendid vestments of the priesthood and practice worship in its outward formalities without life within, but within them is robbery, for He says: “And as troops of robbers wait for a man, so the company of priests murder in the way toward Shechem: for they have committed lewdness” [9]. Let us not be like them, who became robbers of souls, bearing a spirit of murder and destruction while concealed in priestly vestments, bringing ruin into the harbor of peace where people trust them.

1 “When I would have healed Israel, then the iniquity of Ephraim was discovered, and the wickedness of Samaria: for they commit deceit; and the thief cometh in, and the raiders spoil without. 2 And they consider not in their hearts that I remember all their wickedness: now their own doings have beset them about; they are before my face.

When God comes forward as a Physician of souls wishing to heal them, He is compelled to declare the sickness and reveal its extent and gravity so that the sick may accept His treatment. “When I would have healed Israel, then the iniquity of Ephraim was discovered, and the wickedness of Samaria: for they commit deceit; and the thief cometh in, and the raiders spoil without” [1].

He came to heal Israel in general, and so He declared the iniquity of Ephraim, the tribe that took the first place in evil, and exposed the wickedness of Samaria, which is the capital. He is like a physician who does not flatter or temporize but exposes the sickness so that he may stretch out his hand with the scalpel to cut firmly, yet in love. He declares the iniquity of the most wicked tribe and the most corrupt city without flattery at the expense of healing! As for the kind of sickness that struck them, it is “they commit deceit,” and this is the most dangerous thing that can strike a man, that he practice deceit, deceiving people and perhaps deceiving himself and misleading his conscience, thinking that he is able to deceive God also. His heart is full of robbery while his garments are priestly; his city is like Gilead, in appearance containing the men of God, “the Levites,” but in reality containing “them that work iniquity” (Hos 6:8). Thus Israel cloaked its iniquity by presenting offerings and sacrifices to God and practicing some acts of worship, while its heart was far from God and turned away from Him.

If Israel wanted to deceive others with outward appearances, yet the inner corruption bore its reflections on the outward conduct as well, and while it tries to deceive by its appearance it is shattered within and without, for He says: “the thief cometh in, and the raiders spoil without” [1]. The sickness crept in like a thief to the inside, to the hidden depths, and so the door was opened to the raiders outside. Man became corrupt in his entirety, in need of the healing of the heart and thought and intention within, and of treatment of the outward conduct and visible dealings.

The most dangerous thing in their sickness is not the sickness itself but their ignoring of it, for they thought it a trivial matter that does not need to be remembered, and that God Himself does not care about it; therefore He says: “they consider not in their hearts that I remember all their wickedness: now their own doings have beset them about; they are before my face” [2]. If their sins are hidden from their eyes, or do not occupy their thought, yet they stand before the face of God, who remembers them in order to remove them from them.

Perhaps they ask: Why does God declare the iniquity of Ephraim and expose the wickedness of Samaria? He answers: “now their own doings have beset them about” [2]. It is as though He says to them: Do not be angry with me because I uncover your weaknesses, but rather be angry with yourselves because you walk in this way; for even if I expose, it is only to heal your wounds, but you by ignoring them make your sickness incurable!

3 “They make the king glad with their wickedness, and the princes with their lies. 4 They are all adulterers, as an oven heated by the baker, who ceaseth from raising after he hath kneaded the dough, until it be leavened. 5 In the day of our king the princes have made him sick with the heat of wine; he stretched out his hand with scorners. 6 For they have made ready their heart like an oven, whiles they lie in wait: their baker sleepeth all the night; in the morning it burneth as a flaming fire. 7 They are all hot as an oven, and have devoured their judges; all their kings are fallen: there is none among them that calleth unto me.

In chapter four He announced His trial of the priests because of lack of knowledge, and we saw that they represent the heart which, by its impurity, cannot see God, so that it enters with the whole body into the darkness of ignorance and lack of knowledge. Here He condemns the king and the princes, where the king signifies the human will, which by its corruption and evil directs the whole man toward evil and corruption, and the princes signify the centers of leadership in the soul and the energies and gifts they bear.

He says: “They make the king glad with their wickedness, and the princes with their lies” [3]. This is the most hideous picture of leadership, which is not only marked by evil but takes pleasure in the evil and lies of others… Therefore He says: “all their kings are fallen: there is none among them that calleth unto me” [7]. It is as though their gladness does not satisfy their lives nor support their souls, but is a temporary, temporal joy that pushes them to fall and deprives them of resorting to God, so they lose the source of their life and true joy.

He describes these kings and princes (or the inner leaders of man) in their evil thus: “They are all adulterers, as an oven heated by the baker” [4]. The defiled soul becomes like a burning oven, inflamed by evil lusts and uncontrolled passions. St. Jerome says: [“They are all adulterers, their hearts are like an oven” (Septuagint), like an oven which the mercies of God, together with strict fasting, cannot quench (because of their lack of repentance). These are the fiery darts (Eph 6:16) with which Satan wounds men and makes them as though in fire, this fire which the king of Babylon kindled against the three young men… but a fourth appeared in the form of the Son of God, calming the terrible heat and making the flame of the fiery furnace cold.]

St. Jerome holds that this fiery furnace, kindled by evil lusts, can be quenched only by the fiery Holy Spirit, who burns up the corrupt fire in order to kindle God’s holy fire within the heart, for he says: [If the heart were not kindled by the Holy Spirit it could not overcome lust, for the Spirit of the Lord kindled it and burned up the fire of lust]! He also speaks of the holy fire, saying: [Let us pray to the Lord who turns any hardness in us into gentleness, and blots out our sins, so that we become like fire, the coldness of the devil in our heart is removed from us and we grow in the warmth of the Holy Spirit, thus even with the presence also of intense heat of course…]

Not only did they themselves become a burning oven, but even their hidden evil plots and schemes become like the oven: “For they have made ready their heart like an oven, whiles they lie in wait: their baker sleepeth all the night; in the morning it burneth as a flaming fire” [6]. Just as the baker throws wood into the oven and goes to sleep at night and finds it in the morning blazing, so these wicked men throw in fuel, the evil counsels, and in dullness sleep all their night, and at the right time they find the oven blazing.

“They are all hot as an oven, and have devoured their judges” [7]. They devoured the very few righteous who condemn their evil conduct… They became a devouring fire not to evil but to the just judges.

8 “Ephraim, he hath mixed himself among the people; Ephraim is a cake not turned. 9 Strangers have devoured his wealth, and he knoweth it not: yea, gray hairs are sprinkled upon him, yet he knoweth not. 10 And the pride of Israel is humbled in his face: and they do not return to the LORD their God, nor seek him for all this. 11 Ephraim also is like a silly dove without heart: they call to Egypt, they go to Assyria. 12 When they shall go, I will spread my net upon them; I will bring them down as the fowls of the heaven; I will chastise them according to the report of their congregation.
Having uncovered the leaders who became like a heated oven inflamed with the fuel of evil lusts, devouring their righteous judges, He uncovers to the people also their sickness, saying:

A. “Ephraim, he hath mixed himself among the people; Ephraim is a cake not turned” [8]. The boundaries that separate Ephraim from the pagan peoples were removed, although God had earlier affirmed: “The people shall dwell alone” (Num 23:9), but they “were mingled among the heathen, and learned their works” (Ps 106:35). It is a bitter picture of a Church that bears the spirit of the world within her, does not know her obligation as a servant of the Kingdom, but lives with an earthly, temporal mind. Truly it is fitting for the Church not to withdraw from the world in pride nor to take the stance of one who justifies herself, but to bow down like her Lord in love to wash every foot, and open her heart to every person, and show tenderness toward every human being, in order to lift all up to the heavenly life, and not to come down herself to earthly, fleshly thinking.

As for his saying, “a cake not turned,” it refers to the bread that was not turned before being put into the oven, so that its outside appears leavened while the lower part is unleavened; therefore when it enters the oven the upper part cracks while the lower part becomes “heavy and not light.” Thus Ephraim has a religious face when he presents sacrifices and offerings and acts of devotion, but the hidden face bears apostasy from God. Hypocrisy makes man “a cake not turned”: what the public face shows is contrary to what the hidden face bears.

The wicked man, especially the hypocrite, is likened to a cake not turned, which the devil, as a baker, puts into the oven heated and inflamed with the fire of lusts. Whereas the Lord Christ enters with His body into the oven of His divine love, bearing in it the wounds of love and the marks of the Cross in order to present Him to us as “the bread which came down from heaven” (Jn 6), the devil on the contrary wants to catch us in order to put us into the oven of his evil and make of us a cake not turned that he desires and plays with and mocks!

B. “Strangers have devoured his wealth, and he knoweth it not” [9]. Who are these strangers if not the kings of the nations on whom the people of God leaned (relied) to save them, and behold, they devoured them and plundered them of their wealth, as “the king of Syria made them like the dust to be trodden” (2 Kgs 13:7). And as Pharaoh of Egypt also did to them, and the kings of Assyria… so whoever does not return to God his Savior becomes plunder for strangers.

These strangers are in reality the devil and his demons and his works (sins), for they take captive the soul that opens the door to them and plunder from it the most precious thing it has, its eternal life. Thus the devil is counted a stranger because he is not the Creator, yet he claims the world for himself, and wants to possess every soul to make of it a cake not turned, taking it into his oven heated with fire in order to devour it and play with it!

C. “Yea, gray hairs are sprinkled upon him, yet he knoweth not” [9], that is, gray hair spread over their heads and they do not realize… They entered into a state of spiritual old age and came near to decay (Heb 8:13), and as Abba Moses says: [There are some who passed into old age through lukewarmness and sloth.]

But the godly believer’s heart never grows old, but even if his outward man perishes, the inward man is renewed day by day (2 Cor 4:16); he is like the eagle whose youth is renewed (Ps 103:5). Such a one bears not the gray hair of the head or the heart that shatters the body or the soul, but the gray hair of wisdom, that is, its long experience, as the wise man says: “For the gray hair of man is prudence, and the age of old age is the unblemished life; it is not by gray hair of the head but by the wisdom of the virtuous life, and the attaining of the way of perfection in Christ Jesus our Lord.

D. Their fall into pride and self-reliance instead of reliance on God: “And the pride of Israel is humbled in his face: and they do not return to the LORD their God, nor seek him for all this” [10], which He had reproved them for earlier (Hos 5:5).

E. “Ephraim also is like a silly dove without heart: they call to Egypt, they go to Assyria” [11]. The kingdom of Israel was thus constantly floundering; it left its true nest, “the temple of the Lord in Jerusalem,” and went to Samaria to set up a temple according to its own whim. And behold, now it flounders, at one time going to Pharaoh of Egypt to ally with him against the king of Assyria, and at another doing the opposite, and both exploit it for their own account.

It is a silly dove without dignity or wisdom, and without heart, for it bears no spirit of love for God, who draws it to the heavens in one direction without floundering. But the true Church is a dove in the clefts of the rock (Song 2:14), hidden in the Lord Christ, the Rock of ages, walking with dignity and wisdom and bearing a heart wide enough for the love of the heavenly and earthly alike!

St. Jerome comments on the verse before us, saying: [Note that he compares Ephraim to a foolish dove, since Ephraim left the temple and dwelt in the forests. For doves always live in towers, but Ephraim, my dove, abandoned the temple, left the house to live in the forests, and so came to dwell in the wilderness.]

May we not be like the silly dove that knows no resting place, but enter into the Lord through His holy altar and meet Him in His sacrifice that grants salvation, saying: “Yea, the sparrow hath found an house, and the swallow a nest for herself, where she may lay her young, even thine altars, O LORD of hosts, my King, and my God. Blessed are they that dwell in thy house: they will be ever praising thee” (Ps 84:3-4).

13 “Woe unto them! for they have fled from me: ruin unto them! because they have transgressed against me: though I redeem them, yet they have spoken lies against me. 14 And they have not cried unto me with their heart, when they howled upon their beds: they assemble themselves for corn and wine, and they turn away from me. 15 Though I warned them and strengthened their arms, yet do they imagine mischief against me. 16 They return, but not to the most High: they are like a bow that misses: their princes shall fall by the sword for the rage of their tongue: this shall be their derision in the land of Egypt.

Since the heavenly Physician affirmed the necessity of uncovering the wounds and declaring the sickness, for the leaders as for the people, they could not bear this, and declared their rebellion against Him. “Woe unto them! for they have fled from me: ruin unto them! because they have transgressed against me” [13]. He was gracious to them to heal them, and they counted Him an enemy, and fled from Him as the silly dove flees from the towers to live wandering without shelter, and thereby they insulted God their Shepherd and transgressed against Him. They met His love with disobedience, and His gentleness with enmity, for He rebukes them, saying: “though I redeem them, yet they have spoken lies against me” [13]. What is the lie they spoke against God? When they fell into distress they returned with a lie, and did not return to Him in truth, for they returned to have the distress removed from them, while their hearts clung to deviation… They came for temporal blessings of corn and wine, but their hearts turned away from the Giver of gifts. “And they have not cried unto me with their heart, when they howled upon their beds: they assemble themselves for corn and wine (because the rain was withheld from them), and they turn away from me” [14].

They used to cry out with their lips with many words, while their hearts were far from God, whereas, on the contrary, we see Moses not uttering a word with his lips, and God hears the cries of his inner heart (Ex 14:15) and answers them.

God supports them and strengthens their arms, but they imagine mischief against Him [15]; therefore they do not return to the Most High nor seek Him with their hearts, but only through outward appearances. “They are like a bow that misses”… they gather together and cry out, but instead of striking the enemy with bow and sword they shatter themselves and their inner energies: “their princes shall fall by the sword for the rage of their tongue” [16].
“This shall be their derision in the land of Egypt” [16], for they flee to Pharaoh and take refuge in him, and so become an object of mockery and scorn because God has withdrawn from them.

entries.section: 1. Their discipline by the attack of enemies upon them:

paragraphs.text: 1 "Set the trumpet to thy mouth. He shall come as an eagle against the house of the LORD, because they have transgressed my covenant, and trespassed against my law.
"Set the trumpet to thy mouth. He shall come as an eagle against the house of the LORD" [1].

When God opened the eyes of the prophet's insight, he perceived the bitterness that would befall the people because they refused the remedy from the hand of their true Physician. His soul groaned within him, and he did not know what to do, but God commanded him to take the trumpet and put it to his mouth, for the time of warning had come. He asked him to sound the trumpet so that all the people might gather and see the enemy attacking like a swift eagle that swoops down upon its prey and soars in the air.

Lest the people think that God would not allow them to be taken captive, since they are a people chosen by God, God Himself affirmed, "as an eagle against the house of the LORD." It is as though He were saying: I know that you are the house of God (Heb 3:6), but I have allowed the enemy to swoop down upon you like an eagle because you have corrupted My sanctuary and defiled it. I love My house and dwell in it and keep it by My angels, but I send the enemy upon it like an eagle that swoops down to seize and soar, if you dare against Me and despise My sanctuaries.

1 "Set the trumpet to thy mouth. He shall come as an eagle against the house of the LORD, because they have transgressed my covenant, and trespassed against my law. 2 Israel shall cry unto me, My God, we know thee. 3 Israel hath cast off the thing that is good: the enemy shall pursue him. 4 They have set up kings, but not by me: they have made princes, and I knew it not: of their silver and their gold have they made them idols, that they may be cut off. 5 Thy calf, O Samaria, hath cast thee off; mine anger is kindled against them: how long will it be ere they attain to innocency? 6 For from Israel was it also: the workman made it; therefore it is not God: but the calf of Samaria shall be broken in pieces.

What befalls them, although by God's permission, is something that they themselves bring upon themselves, destroying themselves with their own hands. This is what the Lord declares to them, explaining the reasons for their discipline:

First: He says, "because they have transgressed my covenant, and trespassed against my law" [1]. It is as though He were saying: I chose you as a bride for Myself and made with you the covenant of marriage, but you betrayed the covenant and broke it. I chose you as sons and gave you My law as a fatherly commandment, but you disobeyed My commandment and despised My fatherhood.

Second: At the very time when they betrayed the covenant and disobeyed the commandment, they deceived themselves with an outward show of worship without spirit, for He says: "Israel shall cry unto me, My God, we know thee" [2]. They reject Him by their deeds and their hearts, and seek Him with their lips. They turn their backs to Him in their daily life, but when they gather for worship they cry out to Him, saying, "My God, we know thee," as though they wanted to remind Him that they are the chosen people whom God will not allow to be harmed!

Third: Their betrayal of the marriage covenant, or their disobedience to the fatherly commandment, is not done out of weakness as an incidental matter, but springs from a defiled heart, an evil will, and an inward hatred of the holy life, for He says: "Israel hath cast off the thing that is good: the enemy shall pursue him" [3]. Because Israel hated the holy life, God therefore delivered His house, that is, His people, who ought to have been holy to the Lord, to the king of Assyria, who carried the northern kingdom into captivity; and when Judah hated the Lord, God delivered the kingdom of Judah, with the city of Jerusalem and its temple that it contained, into the hands of Nebuchadnezzar. In any case, if God has known us as His own people, then when we refuse in practice to know Him, He delivers us to discipline, saying to us: "You only have I known of all the families of the earth: therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities" (Amos 3:2).

Fourth: He adds to their hatred of the good the following error: "They have set up kings, but not by me: they have made princes, and I knew it not" [4]. In our study of the previous chapter we saw that the king signifies the human will that reigns over the whole man and controls him, and that the princes signify man's energies and gifts, especially those of leadership. Their setting up of kings from themselves and not from God signifies their living according to their own will, and their ordering the affairs of their lives without resorting to God or seeking His counsel. As for His saying, "they have made princes, and I knew it not," it means that their gifts and energies work not for the sake of the Kingdom of God, so they became strangers to Him, neither knowing God nor deserving that God should know them.

God in His love for us wants us to return to Him in everything, so that we do not set up within us kings or princes without His counsel, but rather do as Jephthah, who "uttered all his words before the LORD in Mizpeh" (Judg 11:11), so that it may not be said of us, "neither look unto the Holy One of Israel" (Isa 31:1). As St. John Chrysostom says: [He longs greatly for us always to take refuge in Him, and to ask everything from Him, and without Him to do nothing and utter no word... For this is the habit of lovers, who ask their beloved to be bound to them, so that they do nothing and utter no word without them.]

What we say concerning the kings and princes within the soul, that is, the human will, energies and gifts, we repeat concerning the Church as the congregation of believers, for it is not fitting to appoint a bishop or a priest without the counsel of the Lord. St. Cyprian wrote in one of his letters about the heretics: [There are undoubtedly bishops who were appointed not according to the will of God, but are like those outside the Church. These were appointed contrary to the order of the Gospel and its tradition, as the Lord said through the prophets: "Woe to the rebellious children, saith the Lord, that they take counsel, but not of me; and make a covenant, but not by my Spirit, that they may add sin to sin" [(Isa 30:1) the Septuagint]]. And he wrote in another letter: [Sometimes unworthy bishops are ordained; these are ordained not according to the will of God but according to human arrangement, so that the ordination takes place in an unlawful and ungodly manner, which grieves God, as was declared in the prophet Hosea.]

The Lord continues His rebuke of His people, saying: "of their silver and their gold have they made them idols, that they may be cut off" [4]. They made images of the pagan gods, and so lost the silver and gold they possessed in order to acquire God's wrath and their own destruction, as though they were buying with their silver and gold what would cut them off and destroy them.

If silver signifies the word of God purified seven times, and gold signifies the spiritual life, then some often misuse the word of God and the spiritual life so that they become for their destruction instead of their spiritual edification, as when they set up the word of preaching, or practice the ascetic life, not in a spirit of humility before God but in a spirit of self-importance for the sake of their own honor.

He also says: "Thy calf, O Samaria, hath cast thee off" [5]. This refers to the beginning of the revolt against the kingdom of David, when Jeroboam split off from the kingdom, and, fearing that the people would turn their hearts back to Jerusalem and kill him and follow Rehoboam king of Judah, he made two calves of gold (1 Kgs 12:28), setting up one in Bethel and the other in Dan, and said to the people: "It is too much for you to go up to Jerusalem: behold thy gods, O Israel, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt" (1 Kgs 12:28). It seems that the setting up of the calves was not at first intended for the worship of idols, but they thought that Jehovah dwelt upon them; gradually, however, it turned into idol worship. It seems that the calf at Dan was moved to Samaria when it became the capital of the northern kingdom. In any case, although God permitted Jeroboam to carry out his counsel against Rehoboam the son of Solomon as a discipline for the sins of Solomon, Jeroboam is condemned for doing this, especially for setting up sanctuaries outside Jerusalem which became dangerous centers for spreading idol worship and its abominations.

The calf of Samaria has gone rancid, or been cast off, having lost its splendor even in the eyes of its worshippers, because it could not save itself nor deliver them from the hand of the king of Assyria. "The calf of Samaria shall be broken in pieces" [6], that is, it will be shattered like an earthen vessel into fragments that cannot be mended. They set up for themselves a god that is the work of their own hands, and it was shattered and shattered them with it. It is a bitter picture of many who make for themselves out of their gold a calf in their Samaria, that is, they set up themselves as gods in their corrupt hearts. This self, having become a god, has taken the place of the living God in the inner Jerusalem, and therefore it falls and is shattered from the height of its arrogance.

God's anger was kindled against them [5], because they took His gold, which He had given them to be their gold, and instead of using it for the glory of God they made with it a calf in their Samaria, without beauty, which is shattered into fragments without remedy... They reject the holy God and cannot endure purity... "How long will it be ere they attain to innocency?" [5].

entries.section: 3. Their loss of satisfaction and joy

paragraphs.text: 7 "For they have sown the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind: it hath no stalk: the bud shall yield no meal: if so be it yield, the strangers shall swallow it up. 8 Israel is swallowed up: now shall they be among the Gentiles as a vessel wherein is no pleasure. 9 For they are gone up to Assyria, a wild ass alone by himself: Ephraim hath hired lovers. 10 Though they have hired among the nations, now will I gather them, and they shall be released a little from the burden of the king of princes.

After announcing their discipline by an enemy who attacks their land and plunders them of everything, and revealing to them the reasons for the discipline, He concluded His speech by declaring that evil does not satisfy man nor give him joy, saying: "They have sown the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind" [7]. They endured hardships in preparing everything for sowing, and behold, they sow wind; and when they wished to reap, they gathered turmoil, anxieties and gloom (the whirlwind). Truly "they labour in vain" (Isa 65:23), "labour for the wind" (Eccl 5:16), "and weary themselves for very vanity" (Hab 2:13). As the Apostle says, those who sow to the flesh reap corruption (Gal 6:8).

"It hath no stalk: the bud shall yield no meal" [7]... They spent all their effort in sowing and planting, but they did not gather a crop that would provide flour for eating. Their crop was like the ears that Pharaoh saw in the dream, exceedingly thin, blasted by the east wind.

"If so be it yield, the strangers shall swallow it up" [7]. Even if it yielded a crop, they cannot make use of it, for strangers plunder all their harvest. They surrendered themselves to strange gods, which do not give but swallow up, and do not bless but defile.

entries.section: 3. Their loss of satisfaction and joy

paragraphs.text: Would that they had lost only their labor in sowing and reaping, so that even what they managed to gather the strangers swallowed up; but they also lost their dignity, and became despised and rejected by the very nations whom they imitated, whose gods they worshipped, and whose evil spirit they followed. "Now shall they be among the Gentiles as a vessel wherein is no pleasure. For they are gone up to Assyria, a wild ass alone by himself" [8-9]. Since they keep pace with the nations in their evil, the nations hold them in contempt, and while they take refuge in Assyria, Assyria looks upon them as a wild ass alone by himself. They became like a wild ass, having lost their gentleness, love and tenderness by separating themselves from their God, the giver of the holy and virtuous life. They bore a spirit of isolation instead of the spirit of love that salts the earth so that it does not corrupt; they became corrupt, good for nothing but to be trodden under foot of men (Mt 5:13).
Sin strips the soul of its spiritual splendor even in the eyes of the wicked, and creates in it a spirit of inner isolation and selfishness instead of true, self-giving love.

entries.section: 3. Their loss of satisfaction and joy

paragraphs.text: "Ephraim hath hired lovers" [9], that is, Ephraim offered much to the nations to win their friendship, but his evil made him lose his awe-inspiring dignity and spiritual beauty even in the eyes of these hirelings. Therefore, at the proper time they did not support Ephraim or Israel but swallowed them up [8], and the need arose not for human flattery but for the strong hand of God, which alone is able to deliver them from the harsh bondage: "Now will I gather them, and they shall be released a little from the burden of the king of princes" [10].

entries.section: 4. Their summons to the first bondage

paragraphs.text: 11 "Because Ephraim hath made many altars to sin, altars shall be unto him to sin. 12 I have written to him the great things of my law, but they were counted as a strange thing. 13 They sacrifice flesh for the sacrifices of mine offerings, and eat it; but the LORD accepteth them not; now will he remember their iniquity, and visit their sins: they shall return to Egypt. 14 For Israel hath forgotten his Maker, and buildeth temples; and Judah hath multiplied fenced cities: but I will send a fire upon his cities, and it shall devour the palaces thereof."

entries.section: 4. Their summons to the first bondage

paragraphs.text: Since they wanted to please the nations and win their friendship and affection, they made for themselves pagan altars on which they practiced abominations side by side with their worship of God. Therefore God rejected their worship and their offerings and counted their sacrifices as mere meat and eating... "They sacrifice flesh for the sacrifices of mine offerings, and eat it; but the LORD accepteth them not" [13]. They left God their Savior and leaned on the nations; therefore God leaves them, and they revert to their first bondage, from which He had delivered them... "For Israel hath forgotten his Maker, and buildeth temples; and Judah hath multiplied fenced cities: but I will send a fire upon his cities, and it shall devour the palaces thereof" [14].

entries.section: 1. The turning of their worship into bread of sorrow

paragraphs.text: 1 Rejoice not, O Israel, for joy, as other people: for thou hast gone a whoring from thy God, thou hast loved a reward upon every cornfloor. 2 The floor and the winepress shall not feed them, and the new wine shall fail in her. 3 They shall not dwell in the LORD'S land; but Ephraim shall return to Egypt, and they shall eat unclean things in Assyria. 4 They shall not offer wine offerings to the LORD, neither shall they be pleasing unto him: their sacrifices shall be unto them as the bread of mourners; all that eat thereof shall be polluted: for their bread for their soul shall not come into the house of the LORD. 5 What will ye do in the solemn day, and in the day of the feast of the LORD? 6 For, lo, they are gone because of destruction: Egypt shall gather them up, Memphis shall bury them: the pleasant places for their silver, nettles shall possess them: thorns shall be in their tabernacles.

"Rejoice not, O Israel, for joy, as other people: for thou hast gone a whoring from thy God, thou hast loved a reward upon every cornfloor. The floor and the winepress shall not feed them, and the new wine shall fail in her" [1-2].

Israel thought that the surrounding peoples, with their idolatrous worship marked by many feasts, abominations and revelry, had more luck and joy than he did, so he longed to imitate these peoples and walk after their pattern. But even if the peoples rejoice and are filled with joy amid abominations... this is only an outward show accompanied by inward grief and gloom. Israel, in imitating these peoples, is counted an adulterer against his God, and so falls under bitter discipline. God chose him as a people for Himself, bound to His holy law, and if he deviated he played the part of an adulteress who deserves stoning. So to this day, whenever a believer falls into sin, discipline comes upon him more swiftly and more severely than it comes upon the wicked, because he is chosen by God and is His son who must submit to His discipline. The psalmist says: "Fret not thyself because of evildoers, neither be thou envious against the workers of iniquity... Delight thyself also in the LORD; and he shall give thee the desires of thine heart" (Ps 37:1, 4).

Man thinks that going after his lusts will satisfy him, saying: "I will go after my lovers, that give me my bread and my water, my wool and my flax, mine oil and my drink" (Hos 2:5). This is the reward that man desires to receive from other gods, preferring it to the Lord's blessing declared in "every cornfloor." He seeks the transient temporal reward rather than the Lord's lasting blessing in the granaries of wheat that satisfy his soul, and so he loses both, for the floor and the winepress do not feed him, and the new wine, in which he thought was his joy and delight, fails him.

Historically, this was fulfilled in the life of this people, who ran after the abominations of the nations around them, and so fell into the captivity of Assyria and were deprived of their freedom, their possessions and the good things of their land, and were also deprived of the worship of the living God; they lost both earthly pleasures and spiritual blessings.

Their deprivation of joy is the natural fruit of their adultery against their God. God does not accept their worship, nor their drink offering of wine (a sign of joy), nor is He pleased with their sacrifices, so their offerings become rejected and unclean because they come from a spiritual adulterer. These offerings turn into "bread of sorrow" that returns to them to eat in bitterness, instead of being received as a pleasing aroma.

entries.section: 1. The turning of their worship into bread of sorrow

paragraphs.text: The punishment does not stop at depriving them of joy and satisfaction, but reaches final expulsion from the Lord's land, which He had formerly given them as a promised land flowing with milk and honey, saying: "They shall not dwell in the LORD'S land," for they are carried into captivity, and there they are deprived of everything: "They shall not offer wine offerings to the LORD, neither shall they be pleasing unto him: their sacrifices shall be unto them as the bread of mourners; all that eat thereof shall be polluted: for their bread for their soul shall not come into the house of the LORD" [4]. In the land of captivity they live as in an unclean land, having nothing pure that they could offer to the holy Lord! They had formerly been in the holy land of the Lord, and when their hearts withdrew outside the house of the Lord and they brought abominations into the sanctuaries, they were driven out of the sanctuaries and deprived of practicing a pure worship acceptable to the Lord.

I say that this is a bitter picture of the unfaithful soul, which the Lord brings in, not to a promised land, but establishing His Kingdom within it, giving it His holy blood as a sign of its salvation and granting it His Spirit dwelling in it. Yet in unfaithfulness it breaks the new covenant and attaches itself to abominations, despising God's surpassing gifts, as the Apostle Paul says: "He that despised Moses' law died without mercy under two or three witnesses: of how much sorer punishment, suppose ye, shall he be thought worthy, who hath trodden under foot the Son of God, and hath counted the blood of the covenant, wherewith he was sanctified, an unholy thing, and hath done despite unto the Spirit of grace?" (Heb 10:28-29)... Such a person loses the gifts that God gave him, and the blessings of the New Covenant become a mystery of judgment and a witness against him. Such a soul, if it offers any worship whatsoever, God does not accept it so long as it persists in its betrayal of the covenant and the uncleanness of its heart, but returns it to the soul as bread of sorrow. Therefore St. John Chrysostom says: [It is not fitting to offer a sacrifice from something unclean, for it is counted as the firstfruits of the other works. Let us offer our hands and feet and mouth and all our members (pure) as the firstfruits of God, so that they may be counted a cause of God's pleasure.]

St. Cyprian speaks of the sacrifices rejected by God and returned to those who offer them as bread of sorrow for them; they are the teachings of the heretics, their worship and their baptism, and he says: [Here He teaches us clearly about those who have been joined to sin altogether, defiled by the sacrifice of an unclean, wicked priest], and he also says: [Here He teaches us about those who unite with condemned leaders, since they are defiled with them by their crimes.]

entries.section: 1. The turning of their worship into bread of sorrow

paragraphs.text: Thus the priests in Israel offered sacrifices to God while their hearts were bound to Baal, so He returned their sacrifices to them as bread of sorrow, and expelled them entirely from the house of the Lord by their captivity to Assyria. And lest the hearers say that what the prophet says is a mere theoretical threat that will not be fulfilled in practice, he continues his speech: "What will ye do in the solemn day, and in the day of the feast of the LORD? For, lo, they are gone because of destruction: Egypt shall gather them up, Memphis shall bury them: the pleasant places for their silver, nettles shall possess them: thorns shall be in their tabernacles" [5-6].

They say: In every season and on the feasts of the Lord we gather in the house of the Lord, rejoicing and exulting with psalms and praises, so how does the prophet say that our sacrifices return to us as bread of sorrow? We spend our days in revelry and joy, not in grief and bitterness. The prophet answers that he sees destruction coming swiftly from Assyria, so they take refuge with Pharaoh of Egypt and flee to the land from which the Lord had formerly released them, to die there in Memphis, its capital (Moph). Thus they lose God's promises to them, which are His word (the silver), and in its place they inherit nettles (rust), and their houses in the Promised Land are laid waste and turned into a wilderness that produces brambles and thorns.

If God offered us promises of silver that does not rust, and established for us spiritual houses in which we dwell joyfully and securely, yet deviation of the heart from Him turns us from silver to rust and from houses to a wilderness with its brambles and thorns! Thus man loses God's inner peace and the gladness and joy of his heart, and even loses his life, to be buried like a stranger in Moph, and his life turns to rust and his inner house to a wilderness!

Symbolically, we may say that silver signifies the soul and the house signifies the body in which the soul dwells, as though, when man runs after temporal joy and revelry like the pagan peoples, with the amusements of the world and the love of luxury, he loses his silver soul, which then rusts, and loses the sanctity of his body, which comes again under the curse, growing thorns and brambles.

entries.section: 2. The arrival of the time of punishment

paragraphs.text: 7 The days of visitation are come, the days of recompence are come; Israel shall know it: the prophet is a fool, the spiritual man is mad, for the multitude of thine iniquity, and the great hatred. 8 The watchman of Ephraim was with my God: but the prophet is a snare of a fowler in all his ways, and hatred in the house of his God. 9 They have deeply corrupted themselves, as in the days of Gibeah: therefore he will remember their iniquity, he will visit their sins.

Israel imagined that it was living in the pleasures of the nations and its own lusts, with joy and revelry, and did not realize that the time of punishment had come: "The days of visitation are come, the days of recompence are come" [7]. The time had come in which Israel is repaid for its evil and the prophets are rewarded for their true witness and for their endurance of reproaches and sufferings from them: "Israel shall know it: the prophet is a fool, the spiritual man is mad, for the multitude of thine iniquity, and the great hatred" [7]. Let Israel know that the one they thought a fool is the bearer of the spirit of wisdom, and the one they counted mad is the man of the Spirit, and that the multitude of its iniquity and the multitude of its hatred corrupted its insight so that it did not recognize the prophet, the man of the Spirit. On the other hand, Israel will discover that the false prophet who flatters them with soft words, saying, "Peace, peace; when there is no peace" (Jer 6:14), is truly the fool, and the one who claimed to be a man of the Spirit is truly mad, since he left Israel in its iniquity, soothing its feelings at the expense of the truth. Thus the true prophet, who may wound with the words of truth for the sake of edification, is distinguished from the deceitful prophet, who is "a snare of a fowler in all his ways" [8]. He catches souls with honeyed words, and is full of hatred against the house of his God [8].

entries.section: 2. The arrival of the time of punishment

paragraphs.text: The time of recompense has come for them to discover that "they have deeply corrupted themselves, as in the days of Gibeah" [9]. A Levite lodged as a stranger at Gibeah, which belongs to Benjamin (Judg 19:14), and the men of the city committed evil with his concubine all the night until the morning, and let her go at the dawning of the day, when she came to the door of the house and gave up her spirit. The man took her and cut her into twelve pieces and sent her throughout all the borders of Israel, that they might see the vileness and abomination that had been in that place (Judg 20:6). If the incident of Gibeah exposed the evil, so the time of recompense comes to expose the hidden things of the people!

10 I found Israel like grapes in the wilderness; I saw your fathers as the firstripe in the fig tree at her first time: but they went to Baalpeor, and separated themselves unto that shame; and their abominations were according as they loved. 11 As for Ephraim, their glory shall fly away like a bird, from the birth, and from the womb, and from the conception. 12 Though they bring up their children, yet will I bereave them, that there shall not be a man left: yea, woe also to them when I depart from them! 13 Ephraim, as I saw Tyrus, is planted in a pleasant place: but Ephraim shall bring forth his children to the murderer. 14 Give them, O LORD: what wilt thou give? give them a miscarrying womb and dry breasts.

Israel lost inner spiritual joy: first, because of their seeking the revelry of the peoples and the amusements of the nations, committing adultery against their God, so their worship turned into bread of sorrow [1, 6]; and second, because the time of recompense had come for them to discover the error of their standards, so that the one they thought mad and a fool proved to be the true prophet, and the one they counted a prophet who soothed their feelings proved to be the mad fool [7, 9]; and the third reason for their loss of joy is the change in the nature of Israel: instead of being grapes in the wilderness and the firstripe of the fig tree, he gave himself up to shame, and became in his nature an abomination through his passion, for He says: "I found Israel like grapes in the wilderness; I saw your fathers as the firstripe in the fig tree at her first time: but they went to Baalpeor, and separated themselves unto that shame; and their abominations were according as they loved" [10]. We have already commented on this passage in the introduction to the book.

Instead of Israel being delicious grapes in the eyes of God in the midst of a barren wilderness, and a firstripe fig, he became by his passion a devoted offering and food for Baal-peor, which means "Baal of debauchery" or "lord of debauchery." He surrendered himself by his passion to Satan, the lord of debauchery, and so turned from the state of fruitfulness that gladdened God and himself to a state of barrenness. His nature turned from a joyful nature to a nature filled with gloom and bitterness of soul.

Their attachment to Baal-peor destroyed their nature and also stripped them of their dignity and brought them into disgrace and shame, so that there is no state of birth among them, for their women do not conceive but are barren; and if they conceive and bear, God Himself bereaves them, pronouncing death upon their children, for He says: "Their glory shall fly away like a bird, from the birth, and from the womb, and from the conception. Though they bring up their children, yet will I bereave them, that there shall not be a man left" [11-12]. Ephraim, in his evil, has become like a bird that flies continually, with no nest in which to settle to lay eggs and have young! It is a painful picture of the man whom sin draws away from his true nest, which is "the altar of the LORD of hosts," to wander in the air without rest, spending the days of his exile without repose or security, and he has no young, that is, no spiritual fruit that immortalizes his name in eternity. This barrenness is the natural fruit of fleeing from the divine nest and turning away from God, the giver of fruit... for when they turn away from Him, He turns away from them, and they fall under the eternal woe: "yea, woe also to them when I depart from them!" [12].

Israel fell into a state of barrenness through its worship of Baal and Ashtaroth, since it believed them to be the gods of fruitfulness and fertility; therefore the prophet says: "Give them, O LORD: what wilt thou give? give them a miscarrying womb and dry breasts" [14].

entries.section: 4. Their expulsion from before the Lord

paragraphs.text: 15 All their wickedness is in Gilgal: for there I hated them: for the wickedness of their doings I will drive them out of mine house, I will love them no more: all their princes are revolters. 16 Ephraim is smitten, their root is dried up, they shall bear no fruit: yea, though they bring forth, yet will I slay even the beloved fruit of their womb. 17 My God will cast them away, because they did not hearken unto him: and they shall be wanderers among the nations.

entries.section: 4. Their expulsion from before the Lord

paragraphs.text: Finally, since Israel ran after Baal and Ashtaroth to give it fertility and fruit, it received the miscarrying womb and the dry breasts... What is more bitter is that God drives it out from before His face and deprives it of His holy house. "For the wickedness of their doings I will drive them out of mine house, I will love them no more" [16], so that it can no longer bear fruit, and if it does bear fruit, the Lord slays it from its beginning in the womb, that is, while it is still an embryo. They despised God and did not hearken to Him, and so He treats them lightly and leaves them wandering among the nations without honor [17]. This is the picture of the soul of every believer who forgets the law of his God and seeks the amusements and delights of the world, and so loses everything and becomes like a wanderer in the world without purpose.

1 Israel is a spreading vine, he bringeth forth fruit unto himself: according to the multitude of his fruit he hath increased the altars; according to the goodness of his land they have made goodly images. 2 Their heart is divided; now shall they be punished: he shall break down their altars, he shall spoil their images. 3 For now they shall say, We have no king, because we feared not the LORD; what then should a king do to us? 4 They have spoken words, swearing falsely in making a covenant: thus judgment springeth up as hemlock in the furrows of the field. 5 The inhabitants of Samaria shall fear because of the calves of Bethaven: for the people thereof shall mourn over it, and the priests thereof shall tremble for the glory thereof, because it is departed from it. 6 It shall be also carried unto Assyria for a present to an enemy king: Ephraim shall receive shame, and Israel shall be ashamed of his own counsel. 7 As for Samaria, her king is cut off as the foam upon the water. 8 The high places also of Aven, the sin of Israel, shall be destroyed: the thorn and the thistle shall come up on their altars; and they shall say to the mountains, Cover us; and to the hills, Fall on us.

God uses many similes to reveal the extent of the corruption of the people when they deviate from God, or the extent of the corruption of the human soul by its apostasy from its Savior. He likened His people to a woman beloved of her friend, and an adulteress (Hos 3:1), a stubborn heifer (Hos 4:16), a lamb feeding in a large place for slaughter (Hos 4:16), those who remove the bound (Hos 5:10), an oven heated by the baker (Hos 7:4), a cake not turned (Hos 7:8), a silly dove without heart (Hos 7:11), a wild ass alone by himself (Hos 8:9), a bird from the birth and from the womb and from the conception (Hos 9:11), Tyre planted in a pleasant place (Hos 9:13), one who feedeth on wind and followeth after the east wind (Hos 12:1)... And here He likens them to the vine for which He provided every possibility of fruitfulness in abundance, but it bore fruit not for Him but for sin and abominations. He says: "Israel is a spreading vine (a grapevine), he bringeth forth fruit unto himself" [1]. It is a spreading vine, and as it is in the Septuagint, "a vine with good branches, its fruit abundant." It is without excuse, for He created it with a good nature and gave it the power to grow, so that it had many branches bearing its fruit, yet it brought forth the fruit for itself, that is, for its own thinking and not in submission to the true Vinedresser.

How wondrous! As much as God gives us possibilities and energies, we use them not for the glory of His name but by our own thinking for the sake of the evil lusts of our flesh, as He says: "according to the multitude of his fruit he hath increased the altars; according to the goodness of his land they have made goodly images (statues)" [1]. Thus man repays God's generosity and tenderness with ingratitude.

"Their heart is divided" [2]: some deviated to one god, and others to another god, and so their hearts were torn; or perhaps their hearts were divided between the love of lusts connected with the worship of Baal and the desire to ease their consciences by practicing the worship of the living God in a formal way without spirit, so that they halted between the two parties. Their heart was no longer upright; therefore they cry to God, but not with all their heart, and so they do not find Him... for a divided heart cannot meet the Holy One or know Him.

The divisions of the inner heart rob it of the fear of the Lord, which has its consequences in the life of the community and of every member in it. As for the community, they lose the fear of the Lord and consequently lose their submission even to temporal authority, so that they have no leader able to manage their affairs, for He says: "For now they shall say, We have no king, because we feared not the LORD; what then should a king do to us?" [3].
