As for the individual member, when through the divisions of his heart he loses the fear of the Lord, he loses his true holy will in the Lord, which is symbolized by the king, and so man behaves like one without a will, living in humiliation to every lust and in submission to evil habits, unable to make a spiritual decision in the Lord to be freed from the devil's enslavement of him... He behaves like one without a king. On the contrary, the believer who is pure in heart, without division, bears authority like a spiritual king, saying to this thought to enter, and it enters, and to that one to go out, and it goes out; by the Lord he controls with power his thoughts, his sights, his feelings and his emotions.

When man loses his spiritual authority and his kingly (heavenly) nature, he turns from a man of God who works into a man of words... "They have spoken words, swearing falsely in making a covenant: thus judgment springeth up as hemlock in the furrows of the field" [4]. They turn into men of words without work, and when they feel their weakness they confirm their words with false oaths that they do not keep, and they make covenants that they break, so that judgment becomes like a plowed, tilled field that grows bitter hemlock. Thus when they gather in the centers of justice (the courts), all swear falsely and make promises and do not keep them, and the places of security turn into bitterness of soul.

So it is with the spreading vine to which God gave many possibilities for bearing fruit: if it curls up around itself to bear fruit for the "ego" and for Baal, refusing to give fruit to the true Vinedresser, it loses the fear of the Lord and enters into a division of the heart, which ends in its being deprived of the king, that is, the holy will, and all authority is taken from it. The matter does not stop there, but its life turns into lamentation and trembling as it loses its inner glory and sees the gods it chose for itself collapse before its eyes. The prophet says: "The inhabitants of Samaria shall fear because of the calves of Bethaven (vanity): for the people thereof shall mourn over it, and the priests thereof shall tremble for the glory thereof, because it is departed from it" [5]. What does he mean by this statement? The inhabitants of the capital, that is, Samaria, look at the calves of Beth-aven, or the house of vanity, and see that it has lost its glory, since the people fell under distress and the calves could not save them; so the people of Samaria fear that what befell Beth-aven will befall them, and the priests are terrified because they lose their dignity and forfeit the offerings.

When the people of Samaria lost their hope in Baal, instead of returning to God with repentance, declaring their sins, they go to the king of Assyria with gifts to appease him, in shame and disgrace... "It shall be also carried unto Assyria for a present to an enemy king" [6].

What is the end of this deviating vine? "Ephraim shall receive shame, and Israel shall be ashamed of his own counsel. As for Samaria, her king is cut off as the foam upon the water. The high places also of Aven, the sin of Israel, shall be destroyed: the thorn and the thistle shall come up on their altars; and they shall say to the mountains, Cover us; and to the hills, Fall on us" [6-8].
In brief, we say that its end comes down to the following:
A. "Ephraim shall receive shame"... The tribe that led the movement to spread idol worship becomes ashamed and disgraced before the rest of the tribes, as the gods appear weak before the enemy.
B. "Israel shall be ashamed of his own counsel": since Israel proposed to appease the king of Assyria with gifts, it is ashamed when it sees Assyria humiliating it and treating it with contempt.

C. "As for Samaria, her king is cut off as the foam upon the water": the kings of Samaria, who split from the house of David in strength and might, became like bubbles on the water, and their kingdom ends in captivity under the authority of Assyria. This is the end of every division or schism, for however many vines man obtains at the beginning, his life ends like bubbles on the face of the water.

D. "The high places of Aven, the sin of Israel, shall be destroyed"; what were in their eyes high places that no one could approach is laid waste, and the glory of the golden calves of Beth-aven collapses, and instead of the banquets that were held there, ruin comes.

E. Man falls under the curse, as "the thorn and the thistle shall come up on their altars"; but on the great day of the Lord they say "to the mountains, Cover us; and to the hills, Fall on us," for "it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God" (Heb 10:36), and as it is said in the book of Revelation: "And they say to the mountains and rocks, Fall on us, and hide us from the face of him that sitteth on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb: for the great day of his wrath is come; and who shall be able to stand?" (Rev 6:16-17).

9 "O Israel, thou hast sinned from the days of Gibeah: there they stood: the battle in Gibeah against the children of iniquity did not overtake them. 10 When I desire, I will chastise them; and peoples shall be gathered against them when they are bound to their two iniquities. 11 And Ephraim is as an heifer that is taught, and loveth to tread out the corn; but I passed over upon her fair neck: I will make Ephraim to ride; Judah shall plow, and Jacob shall break his clods.

God assures us that its corruption did not stop at outward appearance, but touches its inner life; therefore the remedy must also enter into the depth of its nature. He says: "O Israel, thou hast sinned from the days of Gibeah" [9]. It is a long period of more than six centuries during which war was continually waged between the tribes and one another, that is, the danger was not from an external enemy but from inner corruption, and we saw that the men of Gibeah, which belongs to Benjamin, did evil with the daughter of Israel (Judg 19-20). Therefore, if God disciplines them with distress from without, it is not fitting for them to fix their eyes on the distress, but on the inner corruption, so that they may be sanctified by the Lord and He may save them from the distress. "When I desire, I will chastise them; and peoples shall be gathered against them when they are bound to their two iniquities" [10].

Finally He explains how Israel became content with inner humiliation and bowed its neck to the yoke of sin, so that it became like the trained heifer that loves to thresh, bearing the yoke in order to eat from what it threshes [11].

entries.section: 3. The need for a new sowing

paragraphs.text: 12 "Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap according to goodness, break up for yourselves a plowing, for it is time to seek the LORD, till he come and teach you righteousness. 13 Ye have plowed hypocrisy, ye have reaped iniquity, ye have eaten the fruit of lies: because thou didst trust in thy way, in the multitude of thy mighty men. 14 Therefore shall a tumult arise among thy people, and all thy fortresses shall be spoiled, as Shalman spoiled Betharbel in the day of battle: the mother was dashed in pieces upon her children. 15 So shall Bethel do unto you because of your great wickedness: in a morning shall the king of Israel utterly be cut off.

If the vine has become barren because of its inner corruption, there is an urgent need for a new sowing that the Lord Himself plants, giving us the fruit of knowledge and righteousness, for He says: "Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap according to goodness, break up for yourselves a plowing, for it is time to seek the LORD, till he come and teach you righteousness" [12]. The Septuagint puts it more clearly: "Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap the fruit of life, be enlightened with the light of knowledge, seek the Lord until He brings you the fruit of righteousness." If the Lord Christ is "our righteousness," then the time has become suitable for the new sowing, in which the Lord Christ dwells in us, as though He is planted within us to renew our nature, so that we bear the fruit of life, and He opens our eyes by His Holy Spirit so that our insight is enlightened. Thus He affirms, "seek the Lord until He brings you the fruit of righteousness," for the righteousness we receive is not from ourselves but is the work of the Lord in us.

But God does not work in the lazy and the slack; therefore He says: "Sow... reap... be enlightened... seek," affirming our positive role so that we may receive God's work in us. Father Nesteros comments on the phrase "be enlightened with the light of knowledge," saying: [You must persevere with striving in reading, which I see you doing, while seeking with all longing to attain practical, experiential knowledge first, that is, knowledge of conduct, for without it the theoretical purity of which we speak cannot be acquired.]

entries.section: 3. The need for a new sowing

paragraphs.text: Let us seek the Lord Himself, who comes to us with the fruit of His righteousness, and let us not rely on ourselves or our human possibilities, lest we hear the words of rebuke: "Ye have plowed hypocrisy, ye have reaped iniquity, ye have eaten the fruit of lies: because thou didst trust in thy way, in the multitude of thy mighty men" [13]. He who relies on his own way or depends on the multitude of his mighty men is plowing hypocrisy, reaping iniquity and eating lies. Israel relied on its own counsel without returning to God, and so caused the people tumult and disturbance, and lost its fortresses, and its women and children fell under the cruelty of Shalmaneser king of Assyria. "Therefore shall a tumult arise among thy people (loss of peace), and all thy fortresses shall be spoiled (loss of security), as Shalman (Shalmaneser) spoiled Betharbel in the day of battle: the mother was dashed in pieces upon her children" [14]. So every man who relies on himself, his life turns into tumult, and he loses his spiritual fortresses and becomes plunder to the devil, who takes him captive as Shalmaneser took many captive.

entries.section: 3. The need for a new sowing

paragraphs.text: He ends his speech with a threat: "So shall Bethel do unto you because of your great wickedness: in a morning shall the king of Israel utterly be cut off" [15]. It is as though He says that what befalls you is not the doing of the king of Assyria, but the doing of Bethel, which became a snare for you, catching you for pagan abominations. Do not rely on the king of Israel, for he perishes in the morning, that is, he is defeated at the beginning of the battle, falls and does not rise!

1 "When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt. 2 As they called them, so they went from them: they sacrificed unto Baalim, and burned incense to graven images. 3 I taught Ephraim also to go, taking them by their arms; but they knew not that I healed them. 4 I drew them with cords of a man, with bands of love: and I was to them as they that take off the yoke on their jaws, and I laid meat unto them.

At the beginning of this chapter God speaks of Israel, that is, His people, or the human soul, as representing a child beloved by God. He longs to release him from the bondage of Pharaoh of Egypt and to set him free as a son of His. He calls him to Himself that he may receive Him as a father, and takes him by the hands like a nurse full of tenderness to teach him to walk in the way of truth, bandages every wound in his depths that struck him during his bondage, draws him with cords of compassion and binds him with the bond of love, and lifts him like a child to caress him with His gentle cheeks, and stretches out His hand to him to feed him Himself... What surpassing tenderness! He plays the part of a nurse full of tenderness toward the human soul, not leaving it in need of anything until He leads it from weak infancy to maturity.
In greater detail we follow the words of the Lord Himself, who says:

"When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt" [1]. While Israel was a child or a boy who does not understand things, unable to offer anything on his part, God loved him and called him out of the land of bondage, offering him sonship. So also God loved Jacob while he was still in the womb, having done neither good nor evil (Rom 9:11). As the Lord says to Jeremiah the prophet: "Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee; and before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee" (Jer 1:5), and the Apostle Paul affirms that God "first loved us."

God took the initiative and loved His child Israel and released him from the bondage of Pharaoh, but Israel remained in his heart attached to bondage, like the sick man who loves sickness, or the prisoner who does not depart in his heart from the darkness of the prison. So our Lord Jesus Christ released us from the bondage of the devil, the true Pharaoh, granting us through Baptism sonship to the Father in Him, but often our heart returns to the land of bondage and we long for the leeks and onions of Egypt, as the children of Israel did before, when they wept, saying: "We remember the fish, which we did eat in Egypt freely; the cucumbers, and the melons, and the leeks, and the onions, and the garlick: but now our soul is dried away: there is nothing at all, beside this manna, before our eyes" (Num 11:5-6). Their souls dried up from the manna that came down from above, and they longed for the small free fish and the cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions and garlic! No wonder, for when man attaches himself to the earth he becomes earth, and his soul wearies of heavenly things and longs for earthly things; he sees dryness in the heavenly and pleasure and joy of heart in the earthly.

The Evangelist Matthew saw in the divine saying "Out of Egypt have I called my son" a clear and explicit prophecy of the flight of the Lord Christ, the Son of the living God, to our Egypt, which was at that time one of the greatest centers of the Gentiles, to declare His acceptance of all the Gentile peoples, sanctifying our land, so that what was formerly a center of paganism became a place of rest for the Savior of the world. And the Lord still enters our inner Egypt to turn it from its paganism into a sanctuary for Him, in which He sets up His divine altar (Isa 19:19), so that it knows Him and offers Him sacrifice and an offering of love (Isa 19:21), to hear His divine voice: "Blessed be Egypt my people" (Isa 19:25).

We return once more to God's care for His child Israel, whom He called from the land of bondage as a son to Him, to learn the son's attitude toward this care. "As they called them, so they went from them: they sacrificed unto Baalim, and burned incense to graven images" [2]. The Septuagint gives it more clearly, declaring that whenever He called them they went away from before Him, as though they were the stubborn son whom his father calls, offering him every protection, but he refuses and flees from his father's face to his enemy, "Baalim and graven images." From his childhood Israel was stubborn toward God, meeting love with coldness and care with obstinacy. Yet God did not cease from His love, for He says: "I taught Ephraim also to go (taught him to walk), taking them by their arms; but they knew not that I healed them" [3]. He tends them like a nurse who takes the hands of the resisting child to teach him how to walk so that he may become mature. He is loving toward them: "I drew them with cords of a man, with bands of love: and I was to them as they that take off the yoke on their jaws, and I laid meat unto them" [4]. The Septuagint makes clear that He used to lift them like a child to His cheeks and bend down to put the food into their mouths; what love is greater than this? He offered every care as a father so that we may take refuge in Him and He may enter into us, and we may become one with Him. As St. Jerome says: [Christ stands every day at the door of our heart, longing to enter. Let us open our heart to Him wide, and He will enter and be our guest, dwell in us and sup with us.]

5 "He shall not return into the land of Egypt, but the Assyrian shall be his king, because they refused to return. 6 And the sword shall abide on his cities, and shall consume his branches, and devour them, because of their own counsels. 7 And my people are bent to backsliding from me: though they called them to the most High, none at all would exalt him. 8 How shall I make thee, Ephraim? how shall I set thee, Israel? how shall I make thee as Admah? how shall I set thee as Zeboim? mine heart is turned within me, my mercies are kindled together.

"He shall not return into the land of Egypt, but the Assyrian shall be his king" [5]. When Israel met with coldness the care of God, who brought him out of the land of bondage, he longed to return again to the land of bondage to take shelter under the shadow of Pharaoh from the king of Assyria, but even if he flees he will be taken captive under the rule of Assyria, and Assyria will reign over him. This is a picture of mankind's attitude toward God, who calls them in His love, and they disobey Him: they went away from before Him [2], giving Him the back, not the face. Instead of offering Him sacrifices of love they "sacrificed unto Baalim," that is, they sacrifice to one Baal and then return to sacrifice to another and a third, and so on, and do not think of returning to God. So He rebukes them bitterly, saying: "My people are bent (clinging) to backsliding from me"; within them is a strong inclination and attraction toward apostasy. I sent to them those who call them to Me, but they refused to return [5]. In the face of this resistance on Israel's part, God is compelled to discipline, saying: "How shall I make thee, Ephraim? how shall I set thee, Israel? how shall I make thee as Admah? how shall I set thee as Zeboim?" [8]. He makes Ephraim and Israel like Admah and Zeboim, two cities in the region of Sodom and Gomorrah that were burned with fire because of their evil.

9 "I will not execute the fierceness of mine anger, I will not return to destroy Ephraim: for I am God, and not man; the Holy One in the midst of thee: and I will not come in wrath. 10 They shall walk after the LORD: he shall roar like a lion: for he shall roar, and the children shall hasten from the west. 11 They shall hasten as a bird out of Egypt, and as a dove out of the land of Assyria: and I will place them in their houses, saith the LORD. 12 Ephraim compasseth me about with lies, and the house of Israel with deceit: but Judah yet strayeth from God, and from the faithful Holy One.

Even in moments of discipline God cannot bear to see His people suffering, for His tender heart turns within Him and the fire of His mercies is kindled in Him, and He is bound to remove the fierceness of His anger from them, saying: "Mine heart is turned within me, my mercies are kindled together. I will not execute the fierceness of mine anger, I will not return to destroy Ephraim: for I am God, and not man; the Holy One in the midst of thee: and I will not come in wrath" [8-9].

If He roars like a lion to discipline firmly [10], His sons hasten to flee, as to Pharaoh of Egypt or the king of Assyria, but in His mercies He returns them, not by their strength nor by their sword, but He returns them in their weakness and helplessness, for "they shall hasten as a bird out of Egypt, and as a dove out of the land of Assyria: and I will place them in their houses, saith the LORD" [11]. By His love He returns them to their houses, so that they return like a bird that has no power or strength, or like a simple dove hastened from the land of enemies to its home. He is the refuge of the weak... He protects the sparrow and supports the dove!

1 "Ephraim feedeth on wind, and followeth after the east wind: he daily increaseth lies and extortion; and they do make a covenant with the Assyrians, and oil is carried into Egypt. 2 The LORD hath also a controversy with Judah, and will punish Jacob according to his ways; according to his doings will he recompense him.

In bitter rebuke He says: "Ephraim feedeth on wind, and followeth after the east wind: he daily increaseth lies and extortion; and they do make a covenant with the Assyrians, and oil is carried into Egypt" [1].

Ephraim forsook his good Shepherd, the giver of true good things, and went out to tend the wind, to acquire nothing. Poor Ephraim, for he toils in tending a wind without benefit... and would that it were any wind, but it is "the east wind." As St. Hippolytus of Rome says, the east wind signifies "the Antichrist," who appears in the East, opposing the Lord Christ in His Church: [What is the burning wind coming from the east but the Antichrist, who shatters and dries up the water-courses and the fruit of the trees in his days (Hos 13:15), since men set their hearts upon his works? He shatters them because of the truth, and they in their hardness serve him]. Thus Ephraim turned from the kingdom of Christ to the Antichrist, and bore the marks of his master: "lies and extortion and making covenants with the world instead of God..."

entries.section: 2. The need for earnestness in returning to Him

paragraphs.text: 3 "In the womb he took his brother by the heel, and in his strength he strove with God. 4 He strove with the angel, and prevailed: he wept, and made supplication unto him: he found him in Bethel, and there he spake with us; 5 even the LORD God of hosts, Jehovah is his name. 6 And thou, return to thy God: keep mercy and truth, and wait on thy God continually.

Since the people take pride in their father "Jacob," He presented him to them as an example of striving with men and with God, who obtained by his striving the meeting with God, who loves those who strive. "In the womb he took his brother by the heel" [3]; while still in his mother's womb, not yet come out into the world, he was striving, and he took hold of his brother's heel to draw him back, seizing from him the birthright and the blessing.

"And in his strength he strove with God, he strove with the angel, and prevailed: he wept, and made supplication unto him" [3-4].. He represents a wonderful example of striving with God, for he gave all his energy to striving with God, who wrestled with him until the dawn to teach him striving and the spirit of victory. And when Jacob realized that the victory was a gift from God and not by his arms, he "wept," and God had mercy on him, revealing Himself to him: "he found him in Bethel, and there he spake with us; even the LORD God of hosts, Jehovah is his name" [4-5].

7 "He is like a Canaanite, the balances of deceit are in his hand: he loveth to oppress. 8 And Ephraim said, Yet I am become rich, I have found me out substance: in all my labours they shall find none iniquity in me that were sin. 9 And I that am the LORD thy God from the land of Egypt will yet make thee to dwell in tabernacles, as in the days of the solemn feast. 10 I have also spoken by the prophets, and I have multiplied visions, and used similitudes, by the ministry of the prophets. 11 Surely they in Gilead have become iniquity, nothing but vanity: in Gilgal they sacrificed bullocks, and their altars are as heaps in the furrows of the field."

The people did not bear the spirit of discernment by which the true Shepherd, the giver of good things, is known from the deceiving shepherds; therefore the Lord requires of them to abandon these standards, contemplating God's true care.

"He is like a Canaanite, the balances of deceit are in his hand: he loveth to oppress" [7]. He lost his nature as a son of God and became like a Gentile without wisdom, a lover of injustice, who slanders God, and even himself. The sign of his deceitful balances is that he thought himself rich and in no need of God: "And Ephraim said, Yet I am become rich, I have found me out substance: in all my labours they shall find none iniquity in me that were sin" [8]. He forgot that God is the one who released him from bondage, sent him the prophets, spoke with him in every way, and trains him: "And I that am the LORD thy God from the land of Egypt will yet make thee to dwell in tabernacles, as in the days of the solemn feast. I have also spoken by the prophets, and I have multiplied visions, and used similitudes, by the ministry of the prophets" [10].

12 And Jacob fled into the wilderness of Aram, and Israel served for a wife, and for a wife he kept sheep. 13 And by a prophet the LORD brought Israel out of Egypt, and by a prophet was he preserved. 14 Ephraim provoked him to anger most bitterly: therefore shall he leave his blood upon him, and his reproach shall his Lord return unto him.

If Jacob their father spent long years in the wilderness of Aram, serving and tending sheep for a wife, is it not fitting for his children to serve in the wilderness of this world for the sake of their Shepherd, the Bridegroom of their souls? He says: "And Jacob fled into the wilderness of Aram, and Israel served for a wife, and for a wife he kept sheep" [12].

1 When Ephraim spake trembling, he exalted himself in Israel; but when he offended in Baal, he died. 2 And now they sin more and more, and have made them molten images of their silver, and idols according to their own understanding, all of it the work of the craftsmen: of them they say, The sacrificers of men kiss the calves. 3 Therefore they shall be as the morning cloud and as the early dew that passeth away, as the chaff that is driven with the whirlwind out of the floor, and as the smoke out of the chimney.

In order to present Himself as a King who saves their souls, He reveals to them what sin, especially the worship of Baal, has done to them, saying: "When Ephraim spake trembling, he exalted himself in Israel; but when he offended in Baal, he died" [1].

When Ephraim walked as his father Jacob walked, in the holy fear of God, he became exalted among the tribes and his standing became prominent, and all were in awe before him. So also those who humble themselves before God, He exalts. But when Ephraim attached himself to Baal in sin, he lost not only his reputation and his awe-inspiring dignity but he "died"... and so he became in need of a mighty Savior able to raise him from the dead.

The strange thing is that sin, with the death it carries, draws man's heart not to remorse over what he has reached, but draws him all the more from sin to sin: "And now they sin more and more" [2]. This causes them to lose the work of God's word in them, since it is "molten images of their silver" [2]; they make it according to their skill or understanding, that is, they set up their gods according to their own whims and do not submit to the mind of God.

They set up idols to worship: "of them they say, The sacrificers of men kiss the calves" [2]. Perhaps he means that because of these idols they tell the priests, who in truth slaughter men by their corruption and uncleanness, to offer on their behalf the most precious of the animals, "the calves," as sacrifices to Baal... For the priests are wicked, and the sacrifices, whatever their value, are an abomination.

He describes those who walk thus, apostate from God their Savior, as those who "shall be as the morning cloud and as the early dew that passeth away, as the chaff that is driven with the whirlwind out of the floor, and as the smoke out of the chimney" [3]. These appear like a cloud that heralds the coming down of rain (a sign of God's grace), but it is the deceptive morning cloud, which as soon as the sun rises disappears altogether. They are like the early dew that quickly vanishes without watering the earth. They are also the light, trivial chaff that is cast about on every side, and like smoke from the chimney (the flue) they quickly disperse and vanish (Ps 68:2).

4 "Yet I am the LORD thy God from the land of Egypt, and thou shalt know no god but me: for there is no saviour beside me. 5 I did know thee in the wilderness, in the land of thirst. 6 When they fed, they were filled; they were filled, and their heart was exalted; therefore have they forgotten me. 7 Therefore I will be unto them as a lion: as a leopard by the way will I lie in wait for them. 8 I will meet them as a bear that is bereaved of her whelps, and will rend the caul of their heart, and there will I devour them like a lioness: the wild beast of the wilderness shall tear them.

Wanting to affirm His saving work for them, He gave them a practical lesson from the life of their fathers, when He delivered them from their bondage to Pharaoh and tended them in the midst of the wilderness until they were satisfied: "Yet I am the LORD thy God from the land of Egypt, and thou shalt know no god but me: for there is no saviour beside me. I did know thee in the wilderness, in the land of thirst. When they fed, they were filled" [4-6]. He satisfied them in the land of thirst when they were in great distress. But when they were satisfied from His hands they denied Him: "they were filled, and their heart was exalted; therefore have they forgotten me" [6].

When the body is satisfied it forgets God its Creator and is lifted up in pride, as it is said in the book of Deuteronomy: "But Jeshurun waxed fat, and kicked: thou art waxen fat, thou art grown thick, thou art covered with fatness; then he forsook God which made him, and lightly esteemed the Rock of his salvation" (Deut 32:15).

Before this denial God stood before them firmly: "Therefore I will be unto them as a lion: as a leopard by the way will I lie in wait for them. I will meet them as a bear that is bereaved of her whelps, and will rend the caul of their heart, and there will I devour them like a lioness: the wild beast of the wilderness shall tear them" [7-8]. As the prophet Isaiah says: "But they rebelled, and vexed his holy Spirit: therefore he was turned to be their enemy, and he fought against them" (Isa 63:10). By this description He revealed the bitterness of God's soul toward His denying children, so that He became to them as an enemy fighting them violently like a lion, watching their movements like a leopard, violently like a bereaved bear, sending upon them chastisements that devour and eat them like a lioness... All this is because they became vessels of wrath fitted to destruction (Rom 9:22).

entries.section: 3. Their rejection of the saving King

paragraphs.text: 9 "Thy destruction, O Israel, is that thou art against me, against thy help. 10 Where now is thy king, that he may save thee in all thy cities? and thy judges, of whom thou saidst, Give me a king and princes? 11 I gave thee a king in mine anger, and took him away in my wrath. 12 The iniquity of Ephraim is bound up; his sin is stored up. 13 The sorrows of a travailing woman shall come upon him: he is an unwise son; for he should not stay long in the place of the breaking forth of children.

"Thy destruction, O Israel, is that thou art against me, against thy help" [9]. According to the translation of the Jesuits, "Destruction is from thee, O Israel, but thy help is in me." What befalls Israel springs from its destructive behavior, which leads it to death, while its salvation is in the rejected King, God their God, whom they forgot, asking for themselves a king after their own desire, as He says to them: "Where now is thy king, that he may save thee in all thy cities? and thy judges, of whom thou saidst, Give me a king and princes? I gave thee a king in mine anger, and took him away in my wrath" [9-11].

Perhaps by this He refers to them when they desired to have a king to judge them like all the nations (1 Sam 8:5), which grieved the heart of Samuel the prophet. Nevertheless God gave them Saul as king according to the desire of their heart, and in His wrath took him from them because of his evils. For our discipline God allows us to obtain what we desire, so that we may realize our need to accept God's will rather than carry out our own will.

entries.section: 3. Their rejection of the saving King

paragraphs.text: They obtained the desire of their heart, a "king" according to their wish, and their iniquity increased: "The iniquity of Ephraim is bound up; his sin is stored up. The sorrows of a travailing woman shall come upon him: he is an unwise son; for he should not stay long in the place of the breaking forth of children" [12-13]. They "treasure up unto themselves wrath against the day of wrath" (Rom 2:5), and so they destroy themselves. Their sins are bound up for their account; God does not forget them, and they are stored in a safe place so that they may give account for them... They thought they were hidden, that no one sees them, that they are forgotten with time, and did not realize that, since they do not remember them seeking forgiveness, they are kept for their destruction. They have become like the woman who carries a child within her, for the labor with its pains is surely coming. But Ephraim, unwisely, fled from contemplating or thinking about the pain that happens because of sin, so as to know the cause of the pain and be delivered from it by God his Savior.
14 "I will ransom them from the power of the grave; I will redeem them from death: O death, where are thy plagues? O grave, where is thy sting? repentance shall be hid from mine eyes."

He who redeemed their fathers from the bondage of Pharaoh is able alone to redeem them even from death and to deliver them from the grave: "I will ransom them from the power of the grave; I will redeem them from death: O death, where are thy plagues? O grave, where is thy sting? repentance shall be hid from mine eyes" [14].

He accomplishes for them what no other king can accomplish for them, for He not only releases them from captivity but has authority to bring them out of the grave and deliver them from death, which was fulfilled by the Savior's entering into death to destroy its authority. As St. Jerome says: [We have this consolation, that the Word of God has slain death... (Our Lord Jesus) died in order that by His death He might put death itself to death.] He also speaks to death, saying: [You have swallowed our Jonah (our Christ), but He is alive even in your belly. You carried Him as dead so that the storm of the world might be calmed and our Nineveh be saved by preaching Him. Yes, He has defeated you and slain you... By His death you have become dead, and by His death we have become alive. You swallowed Him, and behold, you are swallowed up. While you were stricken with desire for the body which He took, seizing it as prey with the claws of your greed, behold, you are wounded within...!.]

This is God's promise to us... He gave us authority over death, without repentance or change in His promise, for He says: "repentance shall be hid from mine eyes," that is, I do not retract what I have promised.

15 "Though he be fruitful among his brethren, an east wind shall come, the wind of the LORD shall come up from the wilderness, and his spring shall become dry, and his fountain shall be dried up: he shall spoil the treasure of all pleasant vessels. 16 Samaria shall be recompensed; for she hath rebelled against her God: they shall fall by the sword: their infants shall be dashed in pieces, and their women with child shall be ripped up."

If the Lord Christ by His death gives life, slaying death, then by divine permission the Antichrist comes and blows as an east wind to dry up within man the spring of the Holy Spirit and make his inner fountain dry and cause him to lose all his fruit: "Though he be fruitful among his brethren, an east wind shall come, the wind of the LORD shall come up from the wilderness, and his spring shall become dry, and his fountain shall be dried up: he shall spoil the treasure of all pleasant vessels. Samaria shall be recompensed; for she hath rebelled against her God: they shall fall by the sword: their infants shall be dashed in pieces, and their women with child shall be ripped up" [15-16]. This speech was fulfilled literally by the blowing of the Assyrian captivity from the east, which destroyed Israel entirely and its capital Samaria, and it will be fulfilled at the end of the ages when the wind of the "Antichrist" blows coming from the east, and it is called "the wind of the LORD" because it is by His permission.

1 O Israel, return unto the LORD thy God; for thou hast fallen by thine iniquity. 2 Take with you words, and turn to the LORD: say unto him, Take away all iniquity, and receive us graciously: so will we render the calves of our lips. 3 Asshur shall not save us; we will not ride upon horses: neither will we say any more to the work of our hands, Ye are our gods: for in thee the fatherless findeth mercy.

The final call came: "Return, O Israel, unto the LORD thy God; for thou hast stumbled by thine iniquity. Take with you words, and turn to the LORD" [1-2]. So our heavenly Bridegroom keeps calling us all the days of our exile, until our last breath, urging us to return to Him. He does not compel us to return by force, but entreats us with His love and draws our heart by His continual calling and declarations. As Abba Mark the Ascetic says: [No power can force us to do good or evil; rather, the one to whom we freely yield our will, whether God or Satan, urges us on to the work that belongs to his kingdom.]

He calls us and keeps on calling us, but He does not compel us, for He esteems our human freedom and deals with us on the level of mutual love, not as lifeless machines in His hands. As St. John Chrysostom says: [We are masters, able to make every member in us an instrument of evil or an instrument of righteousness (in Christ Jesus).] Just as man commits iniquity with full freedom, so it is fitting that he return to the Lord his God with full freedom, asking for divine help to support him in returning.

The first step on the way of repentance is the awareness of error, for He says: "for thou hast stumbled (fallen) by thine iniquity." Therefore it is fitting for you to return to the Lord your God bearing with you "words," which are your confession of the error. For whoever perceives in the depths of his heart that he has fallen because of his iniquity is not at a loss for words, nor does he ask: What shall I confess? Or how shall I confess? For the Holy Spirit, who exposes his iniquities to him, is the One who supports him in confessing them.

Here we want to affirm that confession is not merely a listing of the sins or iniquities we have committed, but first and before everything else it is a feeling of bitterness over what we have done. As Abba Mark the Ascetic says: [The experienced man who learns the truth confesses his sins to God, not by counting up what he has done but by the bitterness of his soul over what he suffers.] And as Fr. John of Kronstadt says: [Let us hasten to entreat God with repentance and tears. Let us enter into ourselves and contemplate our unclean hearts with all exactness, for when we see the multitudes of abominations that hinder the grace of God, we perceive that we are spiritually dead.]

This confession has two complementary aspects: acknowledging the error, and faith in God, the Giver of goodness. As St. Augustine says, we confess our sins to God just as we confess His work in us, praising Him. "Say unto him, Take away all iniquity, and receive us graciously (what is good): so will we render the calves of our lips" [2]. We ask Him to take away from us every iniquity we have committed, and to grant us everything good that comes from Him, which we have lost; the sacrifices of thanksgiving are "the calves of our lips," or the fruit of our lips, according to the Septuagint.

We have perceived the iniquity that killed our heart and put our inner soul to death, and we have confessed God as the Giver of the virtuous life that comes from Him and binds us to Him as the only Savior. So we do not lean on the arm of a man, whatever that arm may be, saying: "Asshur shall not save us; we will not ride upon horses: neither will we say any more to the work of our hands, Ye are our gods." For the people of Israel at that time, this meant realizing that Asshur, on whom they had leaned, did not save them but crushed them and took them captive; that their military power, "the horses," could not rescue them from God's wrath against them because of their wickedness; and that the idols of Baal, which were the work of their hands, were not in truth their gods able to support them. This is one aspect; on the other hand, God wished to declare the separation of the political side from the spiritual side. Salvation is not accomplished by a human arm, however great its might, authority or greatness, like Asshur, nor by temporal power like the horses, nor by gods that are made by our own hands... Rather, salvation is from God. In other words, may we not lean on Asshur, that is, on others, nor on our own power, gifts and personal abilities (the horses), nor on our own righteousness (our inner gods), but say: "in thee the fatherless findeth mercy" [3]. Without You I have become an orphan with no heavenly Father, so who will have mercy on me but You?! As St. Jerome says: [The fatherless are those who have lost God their Father.]

4 I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely: for mine anger is turned away from him. 5 I will be as the dew unto Israel: he shall grow as the lily, and cast forth his roots as Lebanon. 6 His branches shall spread, and his beauty shall be as the olive tree, and his smell as Lebanon. 7 They that dwell under his shadow shall return; they shall revive as the corn, and grow as the vine: the remembrance thereof shall be as the wine of Lebanon. 8 Ephraim shall say, What have I to do any more with idols? I have heard him, and observed him: I am like a green fir tree. From me is thy fruit found. 9 Who is wise, and he shall understand these things? prudent, and he shall know them? for the ways of the LORD are right, and the just shall walk in them: but the hypocrites shall fall therein.
If Israel has come into a diseased condition that is hard, indeed impossible, to cure, then God is the only Physician able to heal him, for He says: "I will heal their backsliding" [4].

And as St. Paphnutius says: [In truth, the saints never say that they have reached that way in which they walk, with progress and perfection in virtue, by their own striving, but by the grace of God, saying: "Lead me in thy truth" (Ps 25:5).]

The Lord comes forward as a true Physician who heals the backsliding soul, and His motive for this work is pure, free love. "I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely (without cost): for mine anger is turned away from him" [4]. The Physician has declared His healing love, saying: "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life" (Jn 3:16).
What has the Physician offered to His beloved patients?
"I will be as the dew unto Israel: he shall grow as the lily, and cast forth his roots as Lebanon.
His branches (his boughs) shall spread, and his beauty shall be as the olive tree, and his smell as Lebanon.
They that dwell under his shadow shall return; they shall revive as the corn, and grow as the vine (the grapevine).
The remembrance thereof shall be as the wine of Lebanon.
Ephraim shall say, What have I to do any more with idols?" [5-8].

In brief, we can say that God offers them Himself as dew coming down from heaven to water them; He refreshes them and makes them like the blooming lily; He renews them inwardly so that their hidden roots go deep; He makes them grow spiritually so that their branches spread without ceasing; He grants them spiritual beauty and glory so that they are like the olive tree in its splendor; He pours out His fragrance upon them so that they have the smell of Lebanon; He uses them for the rest of many, so that many gather under their shadows, and for the joy of many, as they blossom like the vine; and their good remembrance is never cut off.

First: "I will be as the dew unto Israel" [5]. Long ago the Lord said to Moses: "Behold, I will rain bread from heaven for you" (Ex 16:4), and it was said: "And when the dew fell upon the camp in the night, the manna fell upon it" (Num 11:9). But now He does not send bread down to us; rather, He Himself came down to us, offering His holy Body as heavenly bread that satisfies the heart. He came down to us as dew that quenches the flame of the passions, descending upon our inner camp to make it His own camp and dwelling. He comes down by night, in the midst of our darkness, in secret, to turn it into bright day.

When the three youths were cast into the furnace of fire, the Word of God appeared with them, and the furnace became dew for them; likewise, if the world becomes a fire and a furnace, the Lord Christ appears in us and turns our life into dew!

Second: "He shall grow as the lily." The heavenly Bridegroom says: "I am the rose of Sharon, and the lily of the valleys" (Song 2:1), and here He makes His people a blooming lily. As Origen says: [He became the lily of the valleys only so that His beloved too might become a lily, imitating Him... that is, every soul that draws near to Him, follows His steps and imitates Him becomes a lily.] St. Gregory, Bishop of Nyssa, sees that the soul, like the lily, rises straight upward toward the Messiah, its true Vinedresser. He lifts it above the cares of this life and the thorns of sin that choke the soul (Mk 4:18), and raises it above the dust of this life so that it is not defiled. Thus the Lord Christ refreshes His Church, granting her "all spiritual blessings in heavenly places" (Eph 1:3), so that she bears His heavenly traits and fulfills His mission in her.

Third: "and cast forth his roots as Lebanon." If the Church, by clinging to the Lord Christ, comes to bear His uprightness and the fellowship of His nature, and so is counted like Him a lily in the wilderness among the thorns, then the secret of this life is her hidden roots, or her roots that enjoy the work of His grace, so that she bears His life in her and says with the Apostle Paul: "By the grace of God I am what I am: and his grace which was bestowed upon me was not in vain" (1 Cor 15:10).

Fourth: to the extent that the roots strike into the soil to bear "the life of Christ" in it, its visible branches spread out to bear the fruits of the Holy Spirit in abundance, so that it knows no barrenness or fruitlessness.

Fifth: "and his beauty shall be as the olive tree." Thus the believer bears the traits of the Lord and His life through the roots, and the fruits on the branches (the boughs), and also the beauty of the Lord and His glory within and without. As the Lord says to His bride: "and thou wast exceeding beautiful, and thou didst prosper into a kingdom. And thy renown went forth among the heathen for thy beauty: for it was perfect through my comeliness, which I had put upon thee, saith the Lord GOD" (Ezek 16:13-14).

The true believer, while awaiting the fellowship of Christ's glory in eternity, tastes the pledge of this glory or this beauty in his inner life. As St. Macarius the Great says, what he receives afterward is nothing but an extension of the pledge he enjoyed here within himself.

Sixth: "and his smell as Lebanon." When he bears the beauty of God like a fruitful olive tree, the sweet fragrance of Christ appears in him. As the Apostle says: "and maketh manifest the savour of his knowledge by us in every place. For we are unto God a sweet savour of Christ, in them that perish" (2 Cor 2:14-15).

Seventh: "They that dwell under his shadow shall return; they shall revive as the corn, and grow as the vine: the remembrance thereof shall be as the wine of Lebanon." They bear a heart open with love, to gather many under their shadows, offering them spiritual food and gladdening drink, and their way of life remains a good, lasting remembrance that bears witness to their heavenly Bridegroom.

Eighth: "Ephraim shall say, What have I to do any more with idols?!" If Ephraim was the tribe that stirred up the remaining ten tribes to idolatry, it is also the tribe that repents of this deed, declaring its hatred of evil. Thus the energies of evil in man are turned into energies of building for the sake of the kingdom of the true heavenly Bridegroom.

This is a simplified picture of God's work in the life of His people, indeed in the life of each member of them until he returns to Him in repentance and surrenders his life into His hands to work in him. For God responds to our repentance and our return to Him, saying: "I have heard him, and observed him" [8]. It is as though He were watching for our return and observing everything within us, waiting for the slightest movement on our part so that He may move toward us with His love. As the Apostle says: "Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you" (Jas 4:8).

He draws near to us like an evergreen cypress tree, saying to us: "I am like a green fir tree" [8]. He shades us so that the sun of trials cannot harm us. And the Lord assures us that He is the Giver of fruit in our life: "From me is thy fruit found" [8].

Finally, the book closes with advice that He offers to all of us, that we may be wise and return to the Lord in repentance and receive its fruit: "Who is wise, and he shall understand these things? prudent, and he shall know them? for the ways of the LORD are right, and the just shall walk in them: but the hypocrites shall fall therein" [10]. By this He kindles in us the longing to understand the ways of the Lord and to walk in them with wisdom so that we do not stumble. As Father Theophilus, one of the men of the second century, says: [He who has the desire to learn learns much; therefore it is fitting for you to strive to meet with me more in hearing the living voice, that you may grasp the truth with all exactness.]
